paragraphs.text: I. On the Complaint of Job and on the Weakness of Man

In many places divine Scripture shows that we must undergo many disturbances in this life. It also shows that many consolations are at hand. By these a mind that is capable of strength and conscious of what is right should swallow up the troubles of the present and look to the things that hold unending joy. For the consolations outweigh the disturbances, since they bring both relief in present things and hope of things to come. That is why the apostle Paul says: “The sufferings of this time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to come.” They are unworthy, that is, when set in comparison with the consolation, but not with respect to the fruit of redemption.

For whose life on earth is so illustrious that it could equal that heavenly glory? What is more sublime than Paul, who underwent so many dangers and swallowed so much pain and weakness? In the sufferings he underwent for the name of Christ he died daily, as he himself says. Yet he judged that he endured nothing in this time that was out of proportion to the hope and expectation of so great a glory. Elijah endured famine, plots, the terrors of death and the bitterness of toil. And yet he alone, brought down from heaven to earth by fiery chariots and fiery horses and carried back from earth to heaven, outshone all the merit of this service and raised the grace of the devout rider beyond everything human. And what shall I say of Peter? He judged his cross unworthy of the reward to come and asked to be hung head downward, so as to add something to his passion. He was not afraid to heap up its torments on himself.

It was with good reason, then, that holy David testified that he was hastening toward that glory. He did so in the rest of his work, but above all in the forty-first psalm, where he says: “When shall I come and appear before the face of God?” In this psalm he clearly set out both the disturbances of human frailty and the consolations that come from the Lord. In it he also pleads with God on our behalf. He complains that God has forgotten his own work and forgotten the generosity and grace he bestowed on man, whom he had undertaken to protect and adorn. God has abandoned him and cast him off, weak and shipwrecked, to be worn down by various infirmities. Holy Job had done the same before him, but David did it with more restraint and Job with more vehemence. We have resolved, then, to consider the complaints of both, because in them the pattern of human life is set out, its case is pleaded, and its privilege is defined. We must therefore examine them in their order.

Job had lost his children and everything he had except his wife, who alone had been spared him as a temptation. He was also covered with a grievous sore. When he saw that his friends had come not to console him but to magnify and pile up his pain, he perceived that the Lord had given the adversary power to test him. He felt the arrows of the Lord in his body and said that he was pierced by them. Yet like a good athlete, who would not yield to pain or refuse the hardships of the contest, he added: “Though the Lord begin by wounding me, let him not destroy me in the end. For what is my strength, that I

should endure, or what is my time, that my soul should bear it? Is my strength the strength of stones, or is my flesh made of bronze? Or did I not trust in him? But help has withdrawn from me, and his visitation has despised me.”

“Is not the life of man on earth a trial, and his life like that of a day laborer? Or like a servant who fears his master and covers himself in the shade, or like a hired man waiting for his wages? So I too have waited through empty months, and nights of pain have been given to me. If I lie down, I say: When will it be day? If I rise, I say again: When will it be evening? I am full of pain from evening until morning. My body ferments in the rottenness of worms, and I dissolve clods of earth as I scrape the pus from my sores. My life is lighter than a tale; it perishes in empty hope. I will say: My bed will comfort me. But you terrify me in dreams and strike me down with visions.”

How wretched is the condition of man! Like a hireling it labors for others and is itself in want, and it cannot sustain itself except by another’s mercy. Every day it endures a heavy slavery under dread and fear. So that its master may not catch it, it supposes that it can lie hidden, wandering and fugitive, under some shade of this world. Consider the man of whom Sirach speaks in Ecclesiasticus: “Every man who transgresses on his bed, scorning and saying in his soul: Who sees me? Darkness surrounds me, and walls. Whom do I fear?” Does he not seem to you to be truly a hireling, who [?] squandered, like that young man in the gospel who, we read, [?] the portion of property he received from his father? Needy and destitute, he began to feed another man’s herds to relieve his hunger, so as to earn his keep by wages. Yet that young man did at last turn back. He returned to his father, and he did not suppress his sins but confessed them. This man, however, thinks he is not seen by the One who sees all things, and believes that his misdeeds can be hidden by darkness. He holds up a shade, but he is wrong to believe himself hidden. The eye of the Lord is brighter than the sun. It detects all hidden things, lights up what is dark, penetrates the conscience of the inmost heart, and descends to the heights and the depths. Vain, then, is the man who thinks himself safe in darkness, since he cannot escape the light that shines in the darkness, which the darkness does not grasp. So he is caught like a runaway and wicked hireling, and he is recognized before he can hide himself. For all things are known to the Lord before he seeks them, not only what has been done but also what is yet to be.

So whoever thinks he can hide his crime perishes in empty hope: that is a tale, not the truth. Indeed, the tale of sinners is hateful, bearing no fruit but groaning. For “the talk of a fool is a burden on the road.” What else is sin but a burden? It weighs down the traveler through this world, who is pressed under the heavy load of his offense. If he did not wish to lie under that burden, he should have listened to the one who says: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you.”

What is more distressing than when the very bed given for everyone’s rest inflicts a heavy wound? For it is then that we usually recall what we have done, and the conscience within is pierced by the goads of its own deeds. That is why Scripture says to such people: “What you say in your hearts, be sorry for on your beds.” This is indeed a remedy for the debt, but it has nonetheless wounded the conscience. Suppose that sleep does at times steal over the weary. Even then we are terrified by dreams and harassed by visions, so that this is no longer rest but punishment. For so the riches of the world pass away, like the dream of one who wakes. A man has risen from the sleep of this body and possessed nothing, and he has lost even what he believed he had.

Picture for me now that rich man who piled up daily gains and profits of every kind and was driven by his desires. Suppose he suddenly comes to his senses and considers within himself that when he dies he will not take everything with him, nor will the glory of his house go down with him. He sees that what he possesses in this life holds some pleasure, but not for the life to come, and he opens his eyes to heavenly things. Does he not seem to you like one who drank in his dreams and thought he had drunk, and feasted in his dreams and thought he had feasted? Then he opened his eyes and realized that his soul had hoped for nothing, and that he is still hungry and still thirsty. For avarice has no limit and is not satisfied by grasping; the more it has acquired, the needier it becomes and the more it is stirred up. So this man too has risen, and the dream is empty.

But let us hear Job speaking again. The friends who had come to console him pressed upon him and harried him with bitter words, as enemies would. For people in hardship and bitterness have one kind of comfort: being free from guilt, so that they do not seem to suffer their misfortunes as the price of wrongdoing. They were eager to take even this away from the holy man. They wanted him to seem the author of his own hardship, as one who had incurred the Lord’s displeasure by grave sins and was enduring these things for his impieties. So they described the punishments of the wicked. The wicked sow vices and reap sorrows for themselves. They perish at God’s command and are destroyed by the breath of his anger. He blows upon the houses of clay of those who dwell in them, and they wither. He frustrates the schemes of the crafty and stops the mouth of the unjust. What they asserted was true of the Lord’s power, but it did not fit the merits of so great a man. So he answered them: “Truly I know that it is so.

For how can a mortal be just before the Lord? If he wished to contend with him in judgment, God would not listen to him, so that he could not answer even one word of his with a thousand. For God is wise in understanding, and strong, and great. Who is so hardened that he could stand in his sight? He makes the mountains grow old, and they do not know it, and he overturns them in his anger. He shakes the world from its foundations, and its pillars are moved. He speaks to the sun, and it does not rise, and he sets a seal upon the stars. He alone stretches out the heavens and walks on the sea as on a pavement. He makes the Pleiades and the evening star and the north and the chambers of the south. He does great and unsearchable things, glorious and immense, beyond number. If he passes by me, I shall not see him, and if he goes past me, even then I shall not know it.” With how much louder a trumpet has Job proclaimed the power of the Lord! But in that power lies help for the just, not ruin. And indeed, the passage seems to describe power, but it is rather the mysteries of our redemption that it declares.

For who are the mountains that he made grow old, if not Moses, Aaron, Joshua son of Nun, Gideon, the prophets, and all the books of the Old Testament? The Lord Jesus came and brought a new testament, and what had been old was made old. The Christian was renewed and the Jew grew old; grace was renewed and the letter grew old. He overturned the mountains and turned them around. For he overturned and undermined the understanding according to the letter, and he established the spiritual understanding. So that carnal understanding of the law vanished, and the law became spiritual. That is why the apostle says: “We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal.”

But even he who was carnal became spiritual, as he himself declared: “For I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” These are the mountains, then, that Jesus made grow old, and the Jews do not know it. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty, and they would never still be following Jewish follies. They, then, are the ones who do not know. That is why the Lord Jesus says in the gospel: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

But they are not excused for not knowing, since they refuse to know what they ought to have recognized. Certainly we do not begrudge them the pardon, if they follow the Lord’s sentence; but a sentence usually absolves what is past, not what is to come. Nor is he free of crime who crucified the author of his own salvation and afterward did not ask for pardon. Grant that beforehand he did not know whom he was persecuting. Yet when Christ hung on the cross, he ought to have recognized him as Lord of all the elements, for at his death all the elements trembled. The sky was darkened, the sun fled, the earth split apart, the tombs of the dead opened, and the dead rejoined the company of the living. That is why the centurion said: “Truly this was the Son of God.” The centurion acknowledges one who is not his own, while the Levite does not recognize his own; the Gentile worships, while the Hebrew denies. It was with good reason, then, that the pillars of the world were shaken when the chief priests did not believe. But the old pillars were shaken so that new ones might be established, as he himself deigned to say: “I have established its pillars.” Hear which pillars he established: “Peter and James and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave to me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship.”

How, then, can they plead in excuse that they did not know? Some of them saw it, and others learned of it: the sun withdrew before the day had run its course, and came out again before the span of night was over, making night in the day and day in the night. Surely they ought to have understood that the sun withdrew at a command and came out at a command. For the Lord had foretold that he would be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights. The sun learned this and kept the command. So it was in doubt, and said: “What shall I do? When I rise, it is day; when I set, it is night. If I keep my course, I will delay the salvation of the world. Let us hasten toward our own redemption as well. I too must hasten toward new life, for through the benefit of the cross, by which all things are renewed, there will be a new sun and a new heaven. So I hasten, that I may see that Sun of righteousness who lights up the souls of all. But what shall I do? He wills that the resurrection take place after three days. I have found what to do, so that I cause no delay and still keep the number of days. I will not make a whole day and a whole night. I will shorten the hours, so that the Lord Jesus will indeed be among the dead three days and three nights, yet will rise from the dead sooner than the span of three days and nights would allow. So I will shorten the hours once he has mounted the cross. From the sixth hour let night fall at once, so that I may not see the Lord’s passion but may flee the spectacle of a murderous persecution. I will set, and there will be a night of three hours. I will come out and renew the day, so that it lasts three hours. The first day will be completed; the second night will follow in its own span, and a day will follow likewise; the third night will begin, the Lord will rise in the night, and it will be day in the light of the Risen One. So the saying will be fulfilled: ‘And the night shall be lit up like the day.’ This is that great day which Abraham saw and rejoiced, of which David also said: ‘This is the day which the Lord has made; let us exult and rejoice in it.’ I will share in that day not by the service of my labor but in the fruit of exultation.”

The Lord himself, then, will lead the day, and before the end of the world the light of the world will be seen, which enlightens every man coming into this world. He is the Lord who marks and numbers the multitude of the stars. He it is who alone stretches out the heavens, who walked on the sea as on a pavement, when Peter saw him walking and said: “Lord, bid me come to you on the waters.” And the Lord bade him come, but he faltered, and had the Lord not stretched out his right hand to him, he would have sunk beneath the waves and perished. The flesh faltered; the right hand saved. And he said to him: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” So it was faith that walked in the apostle, not the flesh. Indeed, faith faltered, and the flesh had begun to feel shipwreck. This is not said inappropriately, for the flesh is the ship of the soul, as it is written: “Those who go down to the sea in ships”; and elsewhere: “There, pains as of a woman in labor. With a violent wind you will break the ships of Tarshish.” For when our souls are in labor with the Word, they bring forth pains. But once she has given birth, a woman no longer remembers her sorrow because of her joy, since a man has been born to her, the one who redeemed the world. These, then, are the ships of Tarshish, that is, ships to be understood spiritually, which brought gold and silver to Solomon. They are our bodies, which hold treasure in earthen vessels, as the apostle said. Either they are broken even here in the uncertainty of childbirth, as was said: “Woe to those who are pregnant and those who are nursing!” (for when the soul is shaken, the flesh is tossed about), or they will be stirred up when a violent spirit is breathed into them at the resurrection, once the time is fulfilled. As it is written: “Come, Spirit, and breathe upon these dead, and they will live.” That is why Job himself says later on: “For I know that he is eternal and mighty who is to release me, and to raise up on the earth my skin, which has borne these things.” They are broken, moreover, because they are raised up for judgment. But there is a good kind of breaking, for “God does not despise a broken and humbled heart,” and elsewhere: “Heal its breaches.” Yet it was also said to Jehoshaphat: “The ships were broken so that they could not go to Tarshish,” because he had joined himself to a sacrilegious man. So breaking signifies both, since both will take place on the day of judgment. Then all who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God and come forth: those who have done good to the resurrection of life, and those who have done evil to the resurrection of judgment. The prophet David also signifies this when he says: “There, pains as of a woman in labor. As we have heard, so also have we seen, in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God.” For he includes both the pain and the joy to come: pain from the judgment, and joy from the acquittal.
But let us return to the course of the complaint before us.

“He has made many breaches in me,” Job says. “He does not let me breathe; he has filled me with bitterness. And since he is mighty in power, no one can withstand his judgment. If I am just in heart, my tongue goes astray. Wrath destroys the great and the powerful. The wicked die a grievous death, while the just are mocked, for they have been handed over to the ungodly.” Look at each point. The powerful are weighed down by their own wrath, the wicked by their wickedness, and the just by the weakness of the human condition. So nothing is free from danger. A man’s strength and greatness are deceived by his own power, wickedness is afflicted, and virtue is mocked. The one falls because he can do more; the other is afflicted because he can do nothing. The flaw lies in our condition, for our life is swifter than a runner: it has passed by and seen nothing. Like the track of a ship, or of an eagle flying in search of food, so the life of man passes by. What we say we forget, and no mark of our passing is found except that it is full of sorrow and groaning. “I am shaken in all my limbs,” he says. “Would that there were a mediator between us, to reprove and to judge between the two of us.”

“I will say to the Lord: Why do you judge me so? Is it good for you that I should be unjust, because you have rejected the works of your hands and given heed to the counsel of the ungodly? Do you see as a mortal sees? Is your life like a man’s life, or are your years like a man’s years, that you have searched out my iniquities and investigated my sins? For you know that I have not acted impiously; but who is there to rescue me from your hands?” Great is the faith, and great the authority of a conscience, that summons God as witness of its own mind! What belongs to the human condition he does not deny; what belongs to impiety he rejects; what belongs to weakness he confesses. To have sinned belongs to our condition, for no one is free from falling. But acting impiously does not belong to our condition; it is the poison of faithlessness and of a thoroughly wicked mind. The just man does not admit to this. But man’s absolution lies in God’s mercy, not in man’s power.

“Your hands formed me,” he says, “and afterward you turned and struck me down. Remember that you made me of clay and will turn me back into earth. Did you not pour me out like milk and curdle me like cheese? You clothed me with skin and flesh and knit me together with bones and sinews. You put life and mercy in me, and your visitation guarded my spirit.” How great is the holy man’s lament over our common weakness! How great is the authority of his appeal, resting on the fact that God made man with his own hands! The fault is excused on the plea of weakness, and grace is commended by the privilege of God’s eternal workmanship and by his gracious heavenly protection. On this passage David too spoke most beautifully, saying: “What is man, that you are mindful of him, or the son of man, but that you visit him?”
“Having these things in you,” he says, “I know that you can do all things, and nothing is impossible for you.

For if I sin, you will guard me, but you have not made me spotless of iniquity. If I am ungodly, woe to me! If I am just, I cannot lift myself up, for I am full of shame. I am hunted like a lion for the slaughter.” Note three things. “If I sin,” he says, “you will guard me.” And so, O man, confess your sin, that you may obtain pardon. Declare your iniquities, that you may be justified. Why are you ashamed to confess the sins in which you were born? The fault lies with the one who denies what he was born as, not with the one who confesses it. Would that you kept what you have received! Why should you think you have what you have not received? So let the sinner confess, let the ungodly man groan, and let the just man not lift himself up and exalt himself, lest through arrogance he lose the fruit of his righteousness.

And he puts it well: “If I am righteous, I cannot lift myself up, for I am full of confusion.” For the righteous man notices his own frailty more than in [?] … the wise man recognizes it; the fool does not. In fact, the wise man is pierced with remorse at his own lapses, while the fool takes delight in them. The righteous man is his own accuser, the unrighteous man his own defender. The righteous man wants to forestall his accuser by confessing his sin; the unrighteous man longs to hide his sin. The one comes forward at the very start of his speech to own up to his error; the other, in the wordiness of his speech, wraps up the [?] of the accusation so as not to own up to his error.

Again he goes on to say: “Why have you written evil things against me and laid on me the sins of my youth?” He was right to seize on that time of life for his complaint, since it is usually the most slippery toward vice. For childhood has innocence, old age has prudence, and early manhood, the very neighbour of youth, has regard for a good name and shame at doing wrong. Youth alone is weak in strength, unsteady in judgment, hot with vice, scornful of those who counsel it, and easily enticed by pleasures. In so great, so rugged and stormy a whirlwind of this world, why are so many shipwrecks charged against an age that cannot see ahead? That is why David very rightly asked the Lord to pardon him for that whole period of his life, saying: “Remember not the sins of my youth and of my ignorance,” because that is when the heat of the body boils most fiercely and catches fire from the surge of steaming blood.

But let us hear him again. “Mortal man,” he says, “born of woman, is short-lived and full of wrath. Like a flower he has bloomed and fallen; he passes away like a shadow and does not stay. Is not an account required of him too, and have you made him enter into judgment in your sight? For who is clean from filth? No one, even if his life on earth be but a single day.” Truly a wretched condition: that a man should be forced to give an account of a sin he cannot avoid, compelled to enter into judgment and come into the sight of the Lord almighty, and to set out the reasons for the deeds he has run through over so many stages of his life, when no one can be clean from sin, since from the very cradle guilt creeps upon infancy before there is any awareness of wrongdoing. And how wretched too that his life is short, its allurement sweet, its hardship manifold, its anger daily. So in a slight pleasure there is lasting bitterness.

“There is hope for a tree,” he says; “for if it is cut down, it will grow green again, and if its branch has died on the rock, at the scent of water it will flower and bring forth a harvest like a young plant. But a man who has died is gone, and mortal man, once fallen, is no more. And the sea ebbs and flows in its season.” We have seen the course of the prophetic discourse drawn from the two lower elements, earth and sea, which are subject to every injury and to frequent storms. What a powerful argument it has given for our hardship! The shrubs of the earth, he says, and the leafy growth of trees, even when they have died, rise again to living use. The sea too regularly ebbs and flows with the turn of the seasons. But our flesh is always seething; it is its own storm, and it never has a holiday from the onslaught of tempests and pitiable shipwrecks.

“But when he has fallen asleep, he will not rise again until the heaven is sewn up.” This seems to mean: until the heaven is renewed; for there will be a new heaven and a new earth, as it is written. For what is patched is old, and what is old will be changed. Indeed, hear him who says: “In the beginning, Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you remain; they will all grow old like a garment, and like a cloak you will change them, and they will be changed.” We can add this as well: what is old is sewn up, what is new is pressed together. “From the days of John the Baptist the kingdom of heaven is pressed hard, and those who press it take it by force.” So the synagogue was sewing it up in a few, while the Church presses upon it in thousands. Or else it is because the heaven now seems patched, often stitched together in a varied and many-coloured pattern from clouds and mist and the darkness of night and the saffron blush of the rising day — but then “there will be no more night, and they will have no need of lamplight or sunlight, because the Lord will shine upon them,” as John said. Or else it is because “woe to those who sew pillows to overturn the souls of the people.”

The prophet was lamenting the misery of our frailty, which would have no rest in this life and would lose everything at the sudden onset of death. To him the Holy Spirit imparted the knowledge that men would not rise again until there came one who would not patch the old with the new or put a new garment onto an old one, but would make all things new, as he himself said: “Behold, I will make new things.” For he is the resurrection, the firstborn from the dead, in whom we have all indeed received the privilege of the resurrection to come; yet he alone has so far risen with an everlasting resurrection.

So, having heard what God had spoken in him, and having learned through the Holy Spirit that the Son of God would not only come to earth but would also descend to the underworld to raise the dead — which was indeed done at that time as a testimony to those then present and an example to those to come — he turned to the Lord and said: “O that you would keep me in the underworld and hide me until your anger ceases, and appoint me a time when you will remember me! For if a man dies, he will live, completing the days of his life. I will wait until I come to be again. Then you will call me, and I will answer you; do not despise the works of your hands. You have numbered my schemes, and nothing of my sins will escape you. You have sealed up my iniquities in a bag and marked whatever I have unknowingly transgressed.” How sweet a passage, which assures us of the resurrection, and how well it seems to agree with the Lord's words that we read in the Gospel, where he says: “Then they will begin to say to the mountains, ‘Fall on us,’ and to the hills, ‘Cover us.’” For at the consummation of the age the wrath of the Lord will come. Rightly, then, the saint would rather rise for judgment than in the time of divine wrath, which is terrible even to the innocent.

At the same time he is understood to be prophesying, when he says, “appoint me a time when you will remember me,” that he would be raised at the Lord's passion, as is shown at the end of this book. Yet he does not cease to lament, and the more he understands that resurrection is set before him, the more he longs to flee this life, seeing himself handed over into the hands of his adversaries and cast into the power of the wicked, while even his friends have turned into enemies and, when they ought to have comforted him, heap ruin upon ruin. Still, mindful of his pure conscience and clean prayer, he says: “Earth, do not cover over the blood of my flesh,” so that his prayer may rise like incense to the Lord and not linger on the earth. For the prayer of a saint pierces the clouds. But the prayer of a sinner the earth opens its mouth to hide in the blood of the flesh, as God said to Cain the fratricide: “Cursed are you from the earth, which has opened its mouth to receive your brother's blood from your hand, when you till the earth.”

And so the saint tearfully laments the course of this life. “I am perishing,” he says, “and I am carried about by the wind; I beg for burial and do not obtain it. I pray in my distress — and what shall I do? My days have passed in dread; the sinews of my heart are torn apart.” Yet nowhere does he disparage God's judgment, for he knows how deep is the height of the wisdom and knowledge of God, how unsearchable his judgments and untraceable his ways.

“The sons of the boastful,” he says, “have not trodden them, nor has the lion passed through them.” For who could grasp his ways, who has penetrated his hidden secrets? “Where,” he says, “is wisdom found, or what is the place of understanding? Mortal man does not know her way, nor is she found among men. The deep said, ‘She is not in me,’ and the sea said, ‘She is not with me.’” It is not given to you, O man, to know the heights of wisdom; that is why it is written for you: “Do not be high-minded, but fear.” Why are you so curious to search out what it does you no good to know and what you are not granted to learn? Paul heard certain secrets of wisdom that he was forbidden to make known to others, and that is why he was caught up into paradise, caught up as far as the third heaven, to hear things he could not hear while placed on earth. If a man was not allowed to speak of what he heard, how can he inquire into what he has not heard? You are not allowed to know the counsels of the emperor here on earth, and you want to know the counsels of God? You are not allowed to pry too curiously into what is done on earth, and you inquire too curiously into what goes on above heaven? Why do you argue about where wisdom was born? Man does not know her way, nor has perfect wisdom been found among men. It was not in Moses, not in Aaron, not in Joshua son of Nun, not even in David himself, who said, “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom”; for he himself said later, “I have become like a beast of burden before you.” To know the height of wisdom is beyond you, O man; it is enough for you to believe. For “if you do not believe,” he says, “neither will you understand.” You cannot know the deep, you cannot grasp the deep: how will you grasp the height of wisdom? The deep said, “She is not in me” — and can you say that wisdom is in you?

So the deep said, “She is not in me,” because the Lord himself said, “You will not abandon my soul to the underworld.” And the apostle said, “Who will descend into the deep? — that is, to bring Christ up from the dead.” So if the deep is asked, “Where is wisdom?” it answers, “She is not in me, for she has risen.” If the sea is asked, “Where is wisdom?” it says, “She is not with me, for she trod upon me and my waves could not trouble her.” You too, then, set as you are in the strait of this world, do not look for that perfect wisdom of God in this world, because the world did not know her. But if you want to find her, tread on the waves of this world as Peter trod on them, and walk upon the waters of this age. Wisdom will stretch out her right hand to you, as she stretched it out to Peter, for there has been no one whom the waves of this world have not troubled. They troubled Abraham, they troubled Moses, they troubled Peter. Moses crossed through the sea and led an army on foot through the sea, but first he himself was troubled. Peter walked on the waters, but he began to sink in body, because he limped with the step of a weaker faith. So do not look for wisdom in the sea, for the Lord Jesus did not say that he would be with the sea, but with his apostles, so that they might know him at least in part; to them he said: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the world.” Blessed are those with whom he is! Would that he were with us too — but with us is the sea. Peter is with Christ, because he too trod upon the sea; our hearts are set on gold and silver. But wisdom is above gold, not in gold. That is why the one who longed to have wisdom said: “Silver and gold I do not have, but what I have I give you: in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise and walk.” Because he had no gold, he had in the name of Christ the grace of holy works. Therefore it is said to you too: “Draw wisdom into your inmost parts.” “She has been hidden,” he says, “from every man, and concealed from the birds of heaven.” Neither men nor angels knew where she was, for the angels are the birds of heaven, of whom it was said: “And I saw an angel flying through heaven.”

No one could know wisdom, because no one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him. So he revealed it to John, with whom wisdom was, and therefore John spoke not what was his own but what wisdom poured into him: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” Destruction does not know wisdom; malice does not know her. Destruction could not hold her who said, “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” Malice does not know her, because she said, “The wicked will seek me and will not find me.” They can only say, “We have heard of her glory.” God alone knows her. “For God,” he says, “has established her way well; he knows her place.” As for what wisdom's dwelling place is, hear her disciple say: “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has made him known.” For the Son knew the Father, as he himself says: “As the Father knows me, so I know the Father.” Where there is unity of power, the measure of knowledge is equal. So the Father, who knows all things, the weight of the winds and the measure of the waters, himself saw wisdom and made her known through his prophets; for the Father made wisdom known and searched her out, just as the Son, whom nothing escapes, made the Father known. And he said: “O man, why do you want to know the depths of wisdom, which are above you? To fear God is wisdom, and to keep away from evil is understanding.”
II (III). ON THE COMPLAINT OF HOLY JOB

Our earlier discussion concerned the complaint of the saints that the human condition is frail and weak, and has no firmness of its own anywhere except under heaven's protection. Today we must take up the complaint that troubles the common run of people, and many of the wise as well: they see the unjust abounding in good fortune while the just are often afflicted in this world. This is truly slippery ground, where even the saints could scarcely keep their footing in the true view. In fact David himself was disturbed, though he had said earlier, “You have made known to me the hidden things of your wisdom.” Yet afterwards he steadied himself and searched out the way of perfect reasoning. Holy Job too, with those three old friends who had come to comfort him, wrestled over this view in debate. So let us set out the arguments of both men. They are worthy to teach us how to live, since it was in adversity that they earned the right to please God more. Let us, then, hear each of them in turn.

Eliphaz king of the Temanites, Bildad tyrant of the Shuhites and Zophar king of the Minaeans had sharply rebuked holy Job, claiming that he was suffering such great punishment because of his sins. With their feeble understanding they did not notice that the Lord had handed him over to be tested, so that Christ’s athlete, trained by trials, might reach his crown with greater glory. Failing to see so great a mystery of wisdom, and fearing with narrow hearts that they would seem to charge God with injustice for allowing an innocent man to be punished, they turned the blame [?] for the punishments back upon holy Job. They said that the whole life of the wicked is spent in anxiety, and that riches unjustly gathered will be vomited up; that whatever grievous things a man suffers on earth he suffers for his sins; that even if he is prosperous, his good fortune cannot last but vanishes swiftly like a dream, so that his place is not found; that the joy of the wicked is only a heavier fall; and that this is why holy Job too had been changed from prosperity to adversity and, as the price of his offences, had crashed from the heights to the depths. He was mistaken, they said, to claim he was innocent, since the portion of the wicked is such that the Lord’s indignation comes upon him, snows sorrows down on him, and destruction engulfs his house.

Holy Job heard all this, and like a strong athlete sitting on the dung heap, amid all his welts and the cruel pain of his wounds, his whole body covered in dreadful sores, he spoke mysteries. He did not busy himself seeking remedies for his own sickness but gave himself to sacred discourse. And so the sick man’s words were stronger than the words of those who were not sick. They spoke of wrongdoing, but not according to knowledge; they proclaimed God’s judgments, the punishments of the guilty and the rewards of the saints, but they did not know how to tell the guilty from the just. Indeed, the very man whom the Lord God declared just they condemned for injustice and accused of iniquity. So they did not know what fitted each case. But the holy man Job discerned by the Spirit how he ought to speak to each of them; he was therefore stronger than those who appeared sound and unharmed. And why do I say he was found stronger than the others? He was found stronger than himself [he was stronger when sick than when he was well]. For Job sick was stronger than Job healthy had been, as it is written that strength is made perfect in weakness. So Job too, when he was weak, was then the stronger. He was not sick in mind, though he suffered in body, because his soul was not in the flesh, to whose sufferings it did not cling, but in the Spirit, with whose strength it had clothed itself.

That is why he uttered not the groans of the flesh and the weaknesses of the body but the words of the Spirit, words with which to press his attack, not to give ground. At first, indeed, he spoke more gently, to shame them, because they were pressing a just man unjustly, saying that his punishment was less than his sins deserved, and they, sinners themselves, did not blush to accuse an innocent man falsely. “Granted,” he says, “that I have erred, and that the deceiver who pours errors into human minds dwells with me, so that I speak words I ought not, as you say, and my words go astray and my speech comes out at the wrong time: why do you leap on me and revile me, without considering that this trial has come to me from the Lord, who has seen fit to hem me in with a kind of rampart of troubles? I am exercised by adversity, walled in on every side by toil and danger, and still you insult me, wanting to crush the man you ought to help. See, I laugh at reproaches; I will not speak or answer your insults. For it is not you who judge; the one who judges me is the Lord, and the time for his judgment has not yet come. What need is there to cry out before the judgment? It is good to be silent while we wait for the one who judges; it is good not to return insult for insult, so that we too are not counted among the slanderers.”

Let us then imitate this man, who refuted his revilers by his silence. He showed the strength of his spirit, which insults did not move, and he made plain the innocence of his conscience, since he did not recognize the charges as his own but laughed at them as having nothing to do with him. But we, as though the charge really applied to us, make things worse while trying to clear ourselves, and in longing for revenge we confess. Yet Scripture says that you should turn aside a shameful word and take away your garment, for the insolent man passes by. Let us be silent, then, so that he passes by, and so that, provoked, he does not set our garment on fire; for it is written, “Do not kindle the coals of a sinner, lest you be burned in the fire of his flame.” This is why the holy man is silent even when a slave is insolent; even when a poor man reviles him, the just man is silent; even when a sinner hurls abuse, the just man laughs; even when a weak man curses, the just man blesses. David was silent when Gera the son of Shimei cursed him; Job laughed.

Paul blessed, as he himself says: “We are cursed, and we bless.” Under divine teaching, human virtue had advanced and grown, for by then he had come who makes the weak stronger, and Paul had heard him say, “Bless those who curse you, and pray for those who slander you.” What he said in word he proved by example. For when he hung on the cross he said of his persecutors who were reviling him, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing,” so that he prayed for his slanderers, whom he could have forgiven himself. Job, then, laughed, because Christ had not yet come, for whom alone the privilege of the great virtues was reserved, since he himself is the beginning of the virtues, as he said: “The Lord created me the beginning of his ways.”

And laughing, he was silent. He teaches why one must be silent: “I will cry out, and still there is no judgment. He himself,” he says, “has willed that I should suffer these things. Shut in by temptations as by walls, I cannot escape until it pleases God to pull down the heights of my temptations. For if I cry out now, there is still no judgment. I am still in the contest, still wrestling; the struggle still lies ahead of me. The crown has not yet come forth, and no one is crowned unless he has competed according to the rules.”

A third contest was owed him. He had lost all he had, that is, his estate along with his children; his flesh was suffering wounds; it remained for him to overcome the trials of words. That is no small contest. Adam was deceived by speech; Samson was overcome by a word. Nothing pierces the soul like flattering speech, and nothing, again, bites like harsh speech. Many who have overcome the tortures applied to them have not withstood the harshness of words. Job was struggling, but he held out, and he bore the burden of words alongside the burden of wounds. His umpire saw him; from the cloud and the whirlwind he gave the struggling man a hand, declared that his opponents had taken a heavy fall, proclaimed him the winner, and awarded him the crown.

What is finer than to laugh when we are cursed? For we ought to rejoice if what is said does not belong to us. First, because the enemy, wishing to say something against us with which to fasten a charge on us, found nothing true and made up falsehoods in place of truth. Second, because the Lord himself spoke in the Gospel about this kind of accusation, falsely brought against the innocent for the sake of righteousness: “Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven.” So the one who recognizes the charge as true should be silent, so as not to inflame the wound and tear open the scar; and the one who does not recognize it should also be silent, for he is hearing another’s crime, not his own. If he answers back, he makes it his own; if he keeps silent, he turns it back and wounds the reviler. The one who trusts in that promised reward should also be silent, for a man who is not subject to judgment suffers no prejudgment. And even if there is a prejudgment in this world, there will be none at God’s judgment. Finally, so that you may know that insult does not prejudge a good conscience, listen to holy Job say it, surely a weightier witness than if he had held power over the Roman world: “Now I will fall silent and leave off. If I am prejudged now, then I will not be hidden from your face.”

At the outset, then, he answered more sparingly, to remind them of God’s judgment and, like a good physician, to call them back from their insolence and fury and bring them to their senses. But once he saw that they were persisting in their insults, he came back with more and stronger words and struck, as with a heavier fist, those who were stoning an innocent man with the rocks of their words. “Hear,” he says, “hear my words, so that I may not have to seek comfort from you. Bear with me, for I will speak more strongly; the weight of my words will be heavy. I too will speak in line with your view, namely that many in this world abound in a run of good fortune while others are weighed down and placed in hardship, and that this seems to be allotted according to the deserts of sins. But even if I say this, do not laugh, as though I had agreed with you. Even if I am a sinner, I am not answerable to a man, since he who judges and claims power over me is himself under sin. Or if I am judged as a man, that is common to all. I should not be rebuked for it: it is the weakness of our condition, not some particular wickedness.

But tell me: if I suffer this because of my sin, as you allege, why do the wicked live? And not only live, but are filled with riches and multiply their harvests, and enjoy their children too, and their houses overflow?” These things are plainly good in appearance, but by a deeper mystery you will find that what are thought goods are not goods, and what are thought evils are judged better than they.

“They have grown old,” he says, “in riches.” He said pepalaiōntai, so that what is meant seems to be not so much the long possession of riches as the inveterate burden of abundance, just as Ecclesiastes saw riches kept to the harm of their owner, riches that perish amid great strain and anxiety. For what is left behind here perishes and cannot benefit the dead. So the dead man got only anxiety from them and could find no rest, for he left behind what would shame him and took with him nothing he could keep. How unlike the man of whom it is written: “Blessed is the man who has fulfilled his desire from them; he will not be put to shame when he speaks with his enemies in the gate.” His inheritance is the Lord, and his reward comes from the childbearing of the Virgin Mary; at his departure he is praised for his wisdom, since he had nothing to be ashamed of who coveted none of the things of this world. Instead, having stripped off the cast skin of the old man, he wounded the adversary with the spear of self-restraint, so that at the end of this life the adversary, lamed by the wound and confounded with admiration for his virtues, could not raise an outcry against him. So you see that the man who has grown old in the desire for money is not praiseworthy, for he has not been renewed by receiving grace.

Let us look at another point. “Their seed,” he says, “is according to the soul,” that is, they are not counted among the just. For the just sow in the Spirit and from the Spirit will reap eternal life, but those who sow according to the soul cannot reap spiritual things, because the natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God. They are foolishness to him, and he cannot know the things of the Spirit; so he is not filled with spiritual things but is judged.

“Their children are before their eyes,” that is, whatever they do, they do in order to be seen by others, not because they take good counsel to choose what will be approved at the coming judgment. Scripture often uses children to stand for works, because our posterity is richer in good deeds than in children. So Hezekiah too, freed from a grave illness, says: “From this day I will beget children who will proclaim your righteousness, O Lord of my salvation, and I will not cease blessing you with the psaltery all the days of my life.” For devotion and faith are a good posterity, a posterity that did not yield to the captivity which Hezekiah’s sons endured.
And he added, saying that there is no fear among them, no scourge from the Lord.

But the just man says, “For I have been scourged all day long,” and he wants to be scourged so that he may be received by the Lord, and he wants to fear God, because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Nor does he think it happiness if his heifer does not miscarry, as fools think. For what does the ox signify but the toil of farming, which always comes round again and never ends, but just when it seems finished, goes back to the beginning? These are the people who cultivate Sodom and Gomorrah. So those who cultivate Egypt and turn over the clods of the earth with a kind of plough of a dull mind bring forth toil for themselves and reap sorrows. That is why their heifer does not miscarry but gives birth, so that their toil may increase, and all that they conceive they bring forth without the fear of God. But the just glory in a very different way: they glory not in an abundance of riches or in the breeding of livestock but in the Lord, saying, “From fear of you we conceived in the womb, and we have brought forth the spirit of salvation.” Of the just, then, it is said that they have brought forth the spirit of salvation, which they received from the fear of God, not from the wickedness of this world, of which we read: “Behold, he was in labor with injustice; he conceived toil and gave birth to iniquity.” A miscarriage, then, is better than the offspring of worldly people. Indeed, of the man who came into this world and endured its vanity and darkness through a long life, Ecclesiastes declared that a miscarriage is better off than he. For it has more rest than he, because it has not experienced the changes of this world, in which, even if someone has lived a thousand years, he could not see what is good. To have escaped these things, then, is more a matter of grace than to have undergone them.

I. But perhaps someone may be troubled by what he added: that they remain like everlasting sheep, and their children play, taking up the psaltery and the harp, and delight in the sound of a psalm. They have ended their life in good things, and they have fallen asleep in the rest of the underworld. Distinguish these things, and since you are spiritual, judge. The wicked are like the eternal, but not eternal, because they cannot receive eternity from one who is not eternal. He cannot give what he does not have, and one who does not possess light cannot give light. Instead he transforms himself into an angel of light in order to deceive unbelievers. But he transforms himself by a pretence of false light, not by the splendour of everlasting brightness. That is why the Saviour says: I saw Satan falling from heaven like lightning. He is not lightning, but like lightning. Consider some heretic intent on bodily abstinence and on knowledge of the heavenly mysteries. He is thought to be like one who is eternal, yet he does not receive the wages of eternal life, because one who lacks the truth of faith has only a false imitation. His little ones play like the woman who wants to marry once she has grown wanton. She has grown wanton with psaltery and harp, that is, in the sound of the voice and not in the depth of the mysteries, so that it rings out on the lips but brings nothing into the heart.

Such people, then, have ended their life in the good things of the world. That is, they have ended the life they were living, not the one whose reward they hoped for. And so they have fallen asleep in the rest of the underworld, not in the rest of heaven. Let us pray rather to undergo toil here, so that in the kingdom of heaven we may be found worthy to obtain the consolation of eternal rest. For an abundance of prosperity is a great enticement to sin: it lifts a person up into pride and fills him with forgetfulness of his Creator. Consider the rich man in the Gospel who reclined on crimson and purple, and from whose table the righteous poor man Lazarus gathered crumbs. Does that rich man not seem to you to be saying to God: Depart from me; I do not want to know your ways? And truly such people do not want to know the ways of the Lord. If they wanted to, they would know them, but because those ways are full of toil, the lost shun them and turn aside from them. So, like a drunkard, he does not recognize the author of salvation. Then he turns to his drinking companions and says: Let us eat and drink. What profit is there if we serve him? Or what use is it if we keep his commands? This is how a man talks when he is drunk on an abundance of worldly goods, because in this world crimes do not get what they deserve straight away. He lay back at his ease, since everything was at hand for his pleasure. He was conscious of his impiety, but its punishment was being held in reserve, and so he thought that God did not see the crimes of the wicked.

To this opinion of his, therefore, holy Job replied: Do not be careless and at ease, supposing that the Lord's scourges will not come upon you in this very world. Even the lamp of the wicked is put out. It shines for a time, but it does not have eternal light. The world may favour them, because they do the will of him who holds rule in the world, yet a reversal of fortune commonly comes, along with pains from heaven's wrath and indignation, so that they are winnowed like chaff by the wind. The unjust are winnowed like chaff, the just like wheat. Hear the Lord saying to Peter: Behold, Satan has asked to winnow you like wheat; but I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. Those who are winnowed like chaff fail. The one who is like that grain which fell and rose again, heaped up with an increase of much fruit, does not fail. That is why the prophet says: Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at harvest! So impiety is compared to stubble, which is quickly burned up, and to dust. Therefore, after he said: They will be like chaff before the wind, he at once added the verse: or like dust that the wind has carried away. And so that you may know that the wicked man quickly crumbles and vanishes like dust, you have the words of the first psalm: Not so the wicked, not so. That is, they are not like the righteous, but like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth.

He also draws a distinction between the righteous and the wicked. This one, he says, dies in the strength of his simplicity, wholly in abundance and favour; his inward parts are full of fat, and their marrow overflows. But the other ends the course of this life in bitterness of soul and meets his end without having feasted on anything good. What fitting return can be rendered to him for his deserts? He is brought to the grave and keeps watch in his tomb. Even this is no slight punishment: to have no rest in death, and to be carried not to the land of the living but to the tombs of the dead. For one who lives is not sought among the dead; he enjoys eternal life in Abraham's bosom. That is why those two men in shining garments said to the women: Why do you seek the living among the dead?

I. He then lists the crimes of the wicked. They have overstepped boundaries and carried off the flock along with the shepherd. They have led away the orphan's beast of burden and taken the widow's ox in pledge. They have reaped a field not their own, while the weak worked in their vineyards without wages or food. They stripped many of their clothes and made them sleep naked, taking away their soul's covering. These were drenched by the streams from the mountains and, since they had no covering, they sheltered under the rock. Orphans were snatched from their mothers' breasts. The fallen, who ought rather to have been lifted up, were crushed. The hungry were cheated of food, and the souls of little children groaned heavily.

Could he, whom nothing escapes, be ignorant of these things? The underworld lies naked in his sight, and there is no covering for the most wicked, because they cannot hide. He stretches out the north over nothing and hangs the earth upon nothing. He binds up the water in his clouds, and the cloud does not burst beneath his feet. The pillars of heaven sprang apart and trembled at his rebuke. By his power he calmed the sea, and by his discipline he laid low the sea monster. The bars of heaven dread him; by his command he put to death the apostate dragon. Who understands the power of his thunder? Amid such great crimes, then, what hope does the wicked man have? If he trusts in the Lord, will he be saved? I will tell you, he says, what is in the hand of the Lord, and stop adding emptiness to emptiness.

He then describes how wretched the portion of the wicked is. Even if they have many sons, they are without posterity, since they lack a succession of good deeds; for true posterity is not on earth but in heaven. For such men, then, want is their inheritance and death their succession. When they have heaped up riches, they will go begging, because once they are dead they will be in need, since they cannot find rest. No one will pity their widows. They will remain deserted and bereft of the comfort of any union. Even if money is gathered like earth and gold is laid up like clay, their substance will be as empty as a spider's web, and the whole patrimony of their name will be eaten away as if by moths. The rich man lies down and will add nothing more; he opened his eyes and is no more. He remains in pain. Everything in this world, therefore, is nothing. Gold is in the mines, and silver is in the mines: it is dug out of the mine and goes back into the mine. For what is the miser's mind but a mine? Whatever it has received it keeps as though buried, hiding it in the veins and hollows of the earth because it does not know how to use it. Gold is brought out of the mines every day, but who has ever been able to get anything out of a miser?

So the empty hunger for gold profits nothing, because whatever it has gathered slips away. Truly pitiable, then, are those who have deserted the right way and forgotten it, the way with which precious stones cannot be compared at all.

It is hard to search out, impassable to the proud and closed to the boastful, but level for the humble and open to the wise. And so we must seek wisdom, so that we may walk in the right way, along which the adversary could not pass, though he runs through this world like a ravening and roaring lion. Whoever wants to search out wisdom should not seek it in the abyss, like the philosophers, who think that they can come to know its depths of themselves and by their own wit. Nor should he look for it in the sea, for wisdom cannot be where there is tempest and storm wind. Let him seek it instead where there is tranquillity of mind and the peace that is above all understanding.
III (IV). ON THE PLEA OF DAVID.

We have gone through the plea of holy Job. Now let us take up the plea that we find in the Psalms. David himself did not keep silent about the vanity of the world in many places, and he often declared that the things thought to be the goods of this world are empty. He does so especially in Psalm 38, where he says: Yet all things are vanity, every man living. Although man walks in the image of God, he is troubled in vain; he stores up treasure and does not know for whom he gathers it. And elsewhere: How long shall sinners, Lord, how long shall sinners glory? Here they have a shadowy glory! Once they have departed from the world, they can find no fruit of consolation. Yet he also included Psalm 72, in which he himself testifies, under the name of Asaph, that at first he was close to falling, so that he was gripped by no slight grief. He saw sinners in this world overflowing with riches and abounding in prosperity, while he himself, who had kept his heart righteous, was in afflictions and hardships. He testifies that at the beginning he took no slight offence at this. Afterwards, however, he was corrected by the Lord's scourges and enlightened by the grace of divine knowledge, and he learned the order of the true teaching.

I find nowhere, however, that holy Asaph was troubled by any adversities, whereas holy David endured a great many grievous things, full of dangers. He is speaking of his own labours, and so the psalm is inscribed not as being by holy Asaph but as given to holy Asaph, as the title shows. This is made clearer by the Greek psalter, so it appears that David gave the psalm he himself had written to this Asaph, as he did to others, to be sung. But it is written in that very title that the psalms of David have come to an end. How can they have come to an end, when, after these ten psalms have run their course, the titles include psalms of David again, right up to the very end? Let us therefore set aside a question of this kind and consider the sequence of the psalm, taking our start from the first verse of the prophet's plea.

How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart! The progress of his amendment shines out at the very beginning. For no one can truly confess that God is good except one who recognizes his goodness not from the success of his own affairs but from the depth of the heavenly mysteries and the height of the divine plan. That goodness is to be weighed not by how present things appear but by the benefit of things to come. So God is always good to the righteous man, both when he is tormented by bodily pains and when he is afflicted by harsh punishments. He always says: If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure the bad? He rejoices to be crushed here so that he may find consolation in the future, knowing that whoever has received good things in this life already has his reward. One who has not wrestled, who has not been trained in the contest of many battles, will not be able to hope for future rewards.

But whoever is afflicted in this world, whether justly or unjustly, rejoices. Either he is paying the price of his sins here, or he knows that a richer grace awaits him with the Lord if he suffers harsh things unjustly for his name or for some good work. As it is written: There is no glory if you are punished for sinning and endure it; but if you do good and suffer patiently, this is grace with God. For to this you were called, because Christ also died for you, leaving you an example, so that you should follow in his steps. He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth; when he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten. Therefore the righteous man is always righteous, even if he is on the rack, because he justifies God and says that he is suffering less than his sins deserve. He is always wise, for the tortures of the rack do not take away true and perfect wisdom. He does not lose what he is, because by his zeal and resolve of love he casts fear out. As a wise man, he knows how to say that the things we endure in this body are not worthy to be compared with the reward of future glory, and that all the sufferings of this time cannot equal the reward that is to come. God, then, is always good to this man, who knows at what time he will reap. And so, like a good farmer, he ploughs his field here with the ploughshare of a stricter abstinence. Here he roots out weeds with the sickle of the virtues, which cuts away vices. Here he manures it by humbling himself to the ground, knowing that God raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dunghill. Indeed, if the apostle Paul had not counted all things as dung, he could never have gained Christ for himself. Here he guards his fruits, so that he may store them up securely there. So God is always good to him, because he always hopes from God for the things that are good.

Take another point. How good, he says, is the God of Israel to the upright in heart! Is God not good to all, then? He is indeed good to all, because he is the Saviour of all people, especially of believers. That is why the Lord Jesus came to save what was lost, for he came to take away the sin of the world and to heal our wounds. But not all seek the remedy. Many shrink from it for fear that the medicines will sting the force of the ulcer. So he heals the willing and does not compel the unwilling. Those who seek the remedy receive health, but those who reject the physician and do not seek him out cannot feel the physician's goodness, since they do not experience it. The one who is treated is also healed, and so the physician is good to those he has healed. God, then, is good to those whose sins he has forgiven. But how can someone with an incurable sin in the ulcer of his mind think the physician good when he shuns him? So the apostle explained it beautifully, as we said earlier: God is good to all, since he wills all people to be saved, and the special privilege of divine goodness is reserved above all for believers, who are helped by both God's will and his grace. And the psalmist too, by saying: How good is the God of Israel to the upright in heart!
referred it to the judgement of those who know no other way to think of God than that he is good toward all things and in all things.

Then, in the verses that follow, he himself explains what he had felt, saying: But my feet were almost moved; my steps had all but slipped, because I was envious of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners. He certainly does not mean the feet and steps of the body, but the direction and step of the mind, of which he says elsewhere: Let not the foot of pride come to me, and let not the hand of sinners move me. So we must always pray that the Lord will direct the footsteps of our souls, so that they do not slip, and, sliding on some slippery ground of error, become unable to keep their footing. Now the cause of his slipping was that he envied the peace of sinners. But we ought to be zealous for what is good, not for what is full of disgrace, as the apostle Paul also put it when he said: It is good to be zealous in a good thing always. And do not be troubled that he has used "peace" in a bad sense.

Indeed, in the Gospel too you find that there is a peace which Christ rejects, as he himself says: My peace I leave you, my peace I give you; not as the world gives do I give to you. For there is a peace that has no stumbling block, and there is one that has. The peace that comes from love has no stumbling block; the peace that comes from pretence has one. That is why the prophet too says: Peace, peace; and where is peace? Let us flee, then, from the peace of sinners; for they conspire against the innocent, they band together to crush the just man, to destroy the widow or to assault her chastity.

And so there is no reclining for their death. It is not "declining", as most Latin manuscripts have it, but "reclining". For when we toil and bend over some task and stoop, we are accustomed to lean back and rest; but sinners, that is, those guilty of grave offences, and above all the ungodly, cannot lean back. Of them it is said: and bow down their back always. For those who have not clung to Christ do not raise themselves up to heavenly things. And so those whose death is most wretched do not rise again with him, as it is written: The death of sinners is most wretched. But whoever dies with Christ and is buried with him not only leans back to rest but is also raised up. To him the saying aptly applies: You have turned all his bed in his sickness, especially if he is a martyr, whose sickness is dissolved by his suffering, and his death by resurrection.

We have seen that rich man who, clothed in purple and fine linen, reclined at table in this world and feasted splendidly every day, and from whose table poor Lazarus gathered what fell; we have seen how, once placed in torments in hell, he could not lean back, but could barely lift toward Abraham, not his whole self, but only his eyes, begging him to send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool his tongue. So there was no reclining for his death, nor any support in his affliction. For scourges are of no use after death.

And so David, while he was in the life of this body, made himself ready for scourges, so that the Lord might receive him chastened. Consider again, I ask you, holy Job, who was covered with sores, racked in every limb and full of pains throughout his whole body, soaking the clods of earth with the pus and fluid of his wounds: how, since while he was in this body he could not lean back, he found the rest of death. Therefore, knowing his own state, he said: Death is rest to a man. He, then, was not moved under the blow, nor did he waver through any slip of speech, for in all these things he did not sin with his lips, as Scripture testifies; rather, he found a support in his affliction, by which he was strengthened in Christ. So both Job and David, because they were scourged here, had a support in their affliction, for the Father scourges the son whom he receives; but those who are not scourged here are not received there as sons. And so they are not in the toils of men, and they will not be scourged with men, so that they may be scourged for ever with the devil.

Therefore, he says, their pride has held them; they are covered with their iniquity and their ungodliness. Iniquity is an evil garment; if anyone wants to hold it on to us, we must let it go, so that he may not begin to come to judgment with us. And if anyone tries to take away the spiritual tunic we have received, let go the cloak of iniquity and take up the covering of faith and patience, with which David covered himself in fasting, so as not to lose the clothing of virtue. Fasting itself is a covering. Indeed, if the sobriety of fasting had not covered holy Joseph, the wantonness of the adulteress would have stripped him. If Adam had been willing to cover himself with this fast, he would not have been made naked. But because he tasted of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil against the heavenly prohibition, and broke the fast he had been commanded with the food of incontinence, he knew that he was naked. Had he fasted, he would have kept the garments of faith and would not have seen himself uncovered. Let us not, then, clothe ourselves with iniquity and ungodliness, so that it may not be said of any of us: And he clothed himself with cursing.

Adam too clothed himself badly: while he looked for a covering of leaves, he received the sentence of the curse. The Jews clothed themselves with cursing, of whom it is written: Their iniquity has come forth as if from fat; they have passed into the disposition of their heart. For "from fat" is said of what is fatty, that is, rich. Just as a soul fed on good things and stuffed with virtues is filled, as it were, with fat and richness, as it is written, so iniquity that proceeds as if from fat is shown to be not thin and meagre, but full of vices. In short, they did not fall into error by some chance slip, but passed into sacrilege by deliberate counsel and design.

They have set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue has passed over the earth. What it means to set one's mouth against heaven is taught us by the younger of the brothers, who, on returning to his father, said: Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you. And those set their mouth against heaven who think that the responsibility for their crimes is to be laid on some necessity of their birth. Such people are accustomed to spare neither heaven nor earth, so that they suppose a man's life is governed by some course of the stars. They leave nothing to providence, nothing to good conduct. Would that these too had returned like that one of the two young men: the good Lord would not have denied them a remedy. And yet, even if they themselves are unwilling to be healed, the Lord keeps in reserve the grace of return, so that those in Israel who were driven out through the blindness of their own heart may return through the fullness of the Church, and may not spend empty days in this life, but have days full of good works and faith, when the Lord has filled them with spiritual grace. Hear how they are to return: Blindness, he says, has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved. But because the mystery had to be fulfilled, that God should shut up all things in unbelief—that is, should refute and convict them (for when two contend and one gets the upper hand, it is said, "he has shut the other in")—and therefore through his mercy, so that the world might become subject to God, the people did indeed return in its heirs, but was led astray by the error of a late crime [?], so as not to believe that God foreknows hidden things. But the Lord reserved for them the grace of future salvation, so that they may one day be redeemed, saying: Therefore my people shall return hither. What is "hither"? That is: to me, to my equity and justice, to my worship.

And it shall fill the days of its life. You should certainly understand this to mean that the people is indeed redeemed, namely those who have believed. In this, even if those who have not believed are not redeemed, the privilege of redemption is nevertheless conferred on the people of God.

These, then, being in error, said: How does God know? And is there knowledge in the Most High? For they think there is no knowledge in God, because sinners abound in worldly prosperity. And he goes on to bring them in speaking: Behold, these are sinners, and, abounding in this world, they have obtained riches. You have this expressed more plainly in the Gospel, where Simon the Pharisee, seeing that the sinful woman had come into his house and poured ointment on Christ's feet, said within himself: If this man were a prophet, he would surely know who and what sort of woman this is who touches him, that she is a sinner. But God's patience does not prejudge the truth, and his foreknowledge and providence are proved all the more by the very fact that one who lives in sin abounds in the success of worldly prosperity. The stronger man sees this and laughs; the unwary man is led astray and shaken.

Then the psalmist says that he said: So it was in vain that I justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent. That is: I see them abound, I see every advantage go their way, while I am crushed and harried by countless temptations. So it was in vain that I gave myself to innocence and devoted myself to the pursuit of a sober way of life. And he says well, I washed my hands among the innocent, so that he might appear not to claim for himself the height of innocence, but only to offer his diligent effort. Meanwhile he testifies that such words did not go out from him unpunished.

For he records that he was scourged all day long because he had said that he had justified his heart to the Lord in vain; but after the scourges there followed at once the correction of his wrong opinion. For at once, he says, my reproof came in the mornings, that is, in what is open and clear; for the light of truth took hold of him and did not allow him to think what he had said. "And so the light of truth poured into my mind refuted and reproved me, because I had not spoken rightly when I said: In vain have I justified my heart. For I spoke those words as one placed in darkness, and as I recalled them my heart was pricked, and once my heart was pricked my affections were enlightened, so that a blazing fire arose in my heart, which made in me the spiritual beginning of day. Enlightened, then, as the day dawned for me, and set as it were in many mornings, I understood that I had put myself outside the order of the generation of the children of God, since, though at first I had believed that the Maker of the world, providing for the human race, had made all things for our benefit, whether sad or less than pleasing, I later lost so good a conviction, troubled by wrong opinions."

"So I conferred with my heart and said to myself: If I shall speak thus, that I have justified my heart in vain—the voice of God met me, saying: Behold, for the generation of your sons, for which I have made ordinance; that is: Behold, you find in the Scriptures that I have ordained, O Adam, for the generation of your sons, that riches come to the ungodly by chance, not for any merit. Nor are the gains of treasure the rewards of virtue, just as, on the other hand, poverty is not the punishment of sin; but these things come indiscriminately, rolled along like a river in the flood of this world."

"And I reckoned, and seemed to myself to recognize, that this is true, that this accords and agrees with divine providence, and that I had been troubled in vain over things on which I ought not to have dwelt."

"So, because I seemed to myself to have grasped the true view and attained knowledge of the matter itself, I said to myself: This is labour before me, until I enter the sanctuary of God and understand at the last; that is: only this labour remains for me, to enter the sanctuary of God, where the Cherubim are, that is, the depth of knowledge, and not to labour amid uncertainties and opinions." For the talk of a fool is like a burden on the road. Therefore let us enter the inner shrine of sacred knowledge and the innermost recesses of truth, so that there may be no labour in us; for wisdom draws us away from the sense of labour. Indeed, there is no labour in Jacob; the cause of labour is ignorance, since one who does not know that rewards are stored up for the just is not refreshed from his labours, but is rather bowed down and broken by the labour of his own folly. Let us enter, then, the sanctuary of God, where the Cherubim are, in whom is the remembrance of sacred knowledge and of that true and eternal light.

In that lampstand shines an image by which we may understand at the last. For the saint comes to know at the end, and attains perfect wisdom with the progress of age, saying: Lord, make known to me my end, and the number of my days, what it is, that I may know what is lacking to me. What is the end, if not that time when the kingdom is handed over to God the Father, when the hidden things of wisdom are revealed? This end of our contest the prophet was seeking, desiring to know what was lacking to his perfection; for the end of our discipline and studies is perfection.

This, then, is the first principle of true knowledge: that the things of this world happen by chance. The second is this: that because of their evasions you have set before them abundant success in worldly advantages and a wealth of riches, so that they could not plead that it was through poverty and the bitterness of some pain and grief that they were less devout, and that they had been driven by the necessity of want into the guilt of robbery and a passion for plunder.
