For they were not enriched with wealth or raised up with honours for the sake of a tranquil life and the enjoyment of gladness, but so that their complaint might be shut out and their misery heaped up.

Such men, therefore, are cast down while they are raised up. For it is not grace but ruin when no lasting use of the gift is preserved and the excuse for sinning is taken away. For what complaint carries more weight than that divine one you have in the book of the prophet Micah: My people, what have I done to you, or in what have I grieved you, or how have I troubled you? Answer me. Did I not bring you out of the land of Egypt and set you free from the house of bondage? See how the ungodly are cast down while they are lifted up: their complaint is shut out, their punishment heaped up. For, invited by heavenly benefits, they ought not to have deserted the giver of a secure and prosperous life, whom they ought rather to have obeyed. But as God's justice is great, so too is his vengeance severe. For when has the ungodly man ever been accustomed to last? Of him you have it written elsewhere too: I saw the ungodly exalted and lifted up above the cedars of Lebanon, and I passed by, and behold, he was not; and I sought him, and his place was not found. The speed of his extinction is incredible. You see an ungodly man suddenly powerful in this world: while you are passing by, he already is not. For what is a shadow on the earth? How short-lived! Move your foot, and the shadow has passed. Or if something here troubles you, lift the footstep of your mind to the things that are to come, and you will find that the ungodly man, whom you believed to exist here, will not be there; for he who is nothing is not. Indeed, the Lord knows those who are his; but those who are not, he does not acknowledge, because they did not acknowledge him who is.

Of these same men, then, he says here too: They have failed and perished because of their iniquity, like the dream of one awaking. That is: the ungodly fail and vanish like the dream of one just rising from sleep, because they are in darkness and have walked in darkness, and no trace of any good work of theirs remains; they are like those who see a dream. He who dreams, dreams at night, and night is in darkness. The children of darkness are deprived of the sun of justice and the splendour of virtue, always asleep and never awake; of them it is well said: They have slept their sleep and found nothing. For when their souls have been separated from the body, released as it were from the sleep of the body, they will find nothing, they will hold nothing, and they will lose what they thought they held, since the fool and the senseless man, though he has overflowed with riches, will leave his riches to strangers, and the glory of his house will not go down with him to the underworld.

What follows also shows how his image is not found but perishes, since his image is not found in the city of the Lord, that Jerusalem above. For the Lord painted us after his own image and likeness, as he himself teaches, saying: Behold, Jerusalem, I have painted your walls. If we act well, this heavenly image remains in us; if anyone acts wickedly, this image is erased in him—the image, that is, of him who came down from heaven—and there is in him the image of the earthly. Hence the apostle too says: As we have borne the image of the earthly, let us bear also the image of the heavenly. So the images of the good endure and shine in that city of God. But if anyone turns aside to graver sins and does not do penance, his image is abolished or cast out, just as Adam was cast out and shut out of paradise. Whoever, on the other hand, has conducted himself with piety and integrity enters the city of God and brings his image in, so that it may shine in that city of God. Lord, in your city you will bring their images to nothing, because those who have clothed themselves in works of darkness cannot shine in the light. Let us draw an example from the world: see how in cities the images of good princes endure, while the images of tyrants are destroyed.

Considering these things, then, and fixing his mind on them, the holy prophet, who had earlier been troubled, was filled with delight. Hence he himself says: For my heart was delighted, and my kidneys were relaxed. And I was brought to nothing, and I did not know. And I became like a beast of burden before you. And I am always with you. "When I had come to know," he says, "that God cares for human affairs and watches over them, my kidneys found rest"; that is: from the very great weariness of my former folly I found rest through knowing the heavenly good and grace. For the soul too has certain kidneys, which are troubled within us by the labour of ignorance: these are relaxed into rest by the knowledge of heavenly teaching, and, supported as by a prop of heavenly precepts, they are refreshed. "Then," he says, "I understood that I was wearying myself in vain, since I did not know what is true." And I became like a beast of burden.

He did well to add before you; for in comparison with heavenly things, what is man but an irrational beast? Even the stars, bright as they are, vanish at the rising of the sun. And Moses says: I have not been fit since yesterday, since you began to speak with your servant. And, he says, I am weak of voice and slow of speech. So too, then, man—I will not say in comparison with Christ, but in comparison with the angels—seems a dumb beast. Yet let no one despair, for the Lord saves both men and beasts. "And therefore, because I have learned not from myself but from you, I will cling to you always, so that I may cease to be a beast, and you may say to me: But you, stand here with me." For once surrounded by the grace of God, a man begins to be a man who through folly had displayed insensibility and the ignorance of a beast; for a man is proved a man by this, that he is capable of reason and of grace. And so he rejoices that he has been separated from the dumb animals and admitted into the fellowship of men, whom God visits and protects. For what is man, unless it be that the Lord is mindful of him, or that he is visited by the Lord?

Hence, as one visited by him, he says: You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have taken me up. This is how we have received it, and it agrees with the Greek. For the Greek says: ἐκράτησας τῆς χειρός, that is, "you have held the hand", τῆς δεξιᾶς μου, "my right". He is well directed whose right hand God holds in his own hand. He can say: The Lord is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved. If Adam had chosen to have the Lord at his right hand, he would not have been deceived by the serpent. But because he forgot God's command and carried out the serpent's will, the devil held his hand and made him stretch it out to the tree of the knowledge of evil and good, to pluck what was forbidden. In him judgment was passed in advance on all, and the adversary began to stand at the right hand of all. Hence also that form of curse went forth against Judas: And let the devil stand at his right hand. If that curse is grievous, this blessing is very great, by which the bonds of the harsh curse are loosed. That is why the Lord Jesus set the devil at his own right hand, as we read in the book of Zechariah; for he had taken on man's cause and man's place. So he stood where the inheritance of Adam stood. Like a good athlete, he allowed him to stand at his right hand so as to drive him back, saying: Get behind me, Satan. And so the adversary, thrown from his place, withdrew; and so that the devil might not stand at your right hand, he says: Come, follow me. Foreseeing, then, the coming of the Lord, who came down from heaven to free us from the power of the adversary, David says: The Lord is at my right hand, so that I may not be moved. But the one who had the devil at his right hand was moved. Rightly, then, he says here too: You have held my right hand; that is: so that I can no longer sin, so that I, who once wavered with slipping foot, may stand firm in a sure position. How well the apostle said this, when the Lord saw him troubled and, stretching out his right hand, did not let him stagger, but steadied him so that he walked without fear. Once Peter had been rescued, what else did he say but these prophetic verses: You have held my right hand, and in your will you have led me, and with glory you have taken me up? What is the right hand but the active power of the soul? If it is directed by the will of the Lord, it desires nothing else, seeks nothing, and asks for none of the wealth of this world, no supports.

That is why the saint says: “For what is left for me in heaven? And what have I desired on earth besides you?” That is: You are my portion; you are enough for me in all things. I have sought nothing except to have you as my share. I have not submitted myself to any heavenly creature, as the Gentiles do, and I have not craved the riches of this world or the enticements of pleasure. I lack nothing, since I have been taken up by you, and nothing remains in heaven for me to seek beyond this. Having nothing, I have everything, because I have Christ, whom the Most High Father did not spare but handed over for us all; how then has he not given us all things with him? So the Apostle said, for all things are in Christ, through whom are all things and in whom all things hold together. Since I have everything in him, I seek no other reward, for he himself is the reward of all. That is why he said to the one who would be perfect: “Take up your cross and follow me.” Whoever follows him is not led to perfection by a prize; rather, he is brought by perfection to the prize. For those who imitate Christ do so not in hope of some good but out of love for virtue, since Christ is good by nature, not from desire for a reward. He suffered because he delighted in doing good, not because he sought an increase of glory from his suffering. So whoever wants to imitate him works not for what profits himself but for what profits others. Not without reason, then, he fails for himself, yet grows strong for others through the increase of virtue.

And it is fitting that he says: “My heart and my flesh have failed, O God of my heart.” For things eternal cannot take their place unless earthly things have failed. The flesh fails, then, when the things of the flesh are put to death. Those who carry about the dying of Jesus Christ in their flesh also fail, for the death of Christ works in them so that every enticement of error may die. From this we gather that a person's heart also fails when the evil thoughts that come out of the heart are put to death, so that forgetfulness may hide all earthly things, and God may become the God of the heart of those who, blessed in their purity of heart, are found worthy to see God, so that they draw near to you and do not cut themselves off. For God draws near; he does not drive away those who draw near to him, since he wishes to be a cause of salvation for all, not of death. In fact he drives no one away except the one who has thought he should withdraw from his sight. For, he says, “behold, those who go far from you will perish.”

For each person, by his own works, either joins himself to your goodness or separates himself from it. Whoever does things he fears to be caught in once they are known flees from God, like the man who, hidden by walls and wrapped in darkness, thinks the Lord God does not see him. But he is seen, as when it is said: “You have destroyed all who go whoring away from you.” For just as a woman who commits adultery does not cleave to her husband, and is neither one flesh nor one spirit with him, but divides and separates herself by her adultery, so every soul that does not cleave to God, but goes whoring in slavish service to the empty worship of idols, divides itself by the perversity of sacrilege and becomes far from the Lord when it ought to be near. And whoever is separated from the Lord perishes.

That is why the saint, who dreads God's judgment, wishes always to cleave to Christ and to place his hope in him, so as to praise the Lord, to whom be honor, glory and eternity from the ages, both now and always and for all ages of ages. Amen.
Book 4 (2). The Prayer of David.

Many, indeed, have lamented the weakness of our frail human nature, but holy Job and holy David did so more remarkably than the rest. Job, the earlier of the two, is direct, vehement and sharp, and speaks in a loftier, tragic style, as though made bitter by heavy sufferings. David is gentle, calm and mild, with a softer feeling, so that he truly imitated the disposition of the deer, which he had set before himself as a model. Do not be disturbed if I seem to praise so great a prophet by comparing him to a wild animal, since you read what was said to the apostles: “Be wise as serpents and simple as doves.”

Yet although comparisons of this kind are supported by holy examples, and deer are innocent and gentle by nature, I think that the deer set forth here for the prophet to imitate is the one of whom Solomon, who upheld his father’s mind, said in Proverbs: “Let the deer of friendship and the foal of graces converse with you.” For the true Son of God expressed in himself the nature that he himself had given to living creatures. He came into this world like a deer, and with wonderful simplicity he joined himself to those who were laying snares for him. For deer of this kind are said to be so simple that when they see themselves being hunted, they attach themselves to the very horsemen who have been set to serve the deception; these, by pretending to flee and feigning companionship, lure them on and lead them right into the nets. In the same way the Lord, as if unaware of the danger and taking no precaution, mingled with the Jews who were plotting treachery against him, and he took Judas the traitor into his company, whose deadly pretense brought him to the snares of the cross and the nets of the passion. That is why he turned to him and said: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” In this way, then, he came to the nets of the synagogue and willingly put them on; but he was neither entangled nor bound, for he is the one who set everyone free.

So he rose above the nets. And because his own people had not received him, he called the Church and bestowed his grace on her, as the most holy Church herself testifies in the Song of Songs, saying: “I have adjured you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the powers and strengths of the field, that you stir up and awaken love until it please.” She asks, then, by the smell of the field, the smell that holy Jacob gave off—that is, by that faith, by that devotion—that the daughters of Jerusalem should rouse her bridegroom, so that he may hasten to his bride, and that his love may be roused within her, or even that he himself may be roused, since the bridegroom is love; for “God is love,” as John said. But he did not wait to be roused by others; he was hastening of his own accord. Coming forth from his chamber, he rejoiced like a giant to run his course. The bride saw him and heard the voice of the one who was coming, and turning suddenly she said: “Behold, he comes leaping over the mountains, bounding over the hills.” He leaps over the greater ones and bounds over the lesser, so that nothing may hinder his devoted haste. “My kinsman,” she says, “is like a roe or a young stag on the mountains of Bethel.” A good deer, whose mountain is the house of God, toward which he ran with such speed that he outstripped the bride’s prayers and longings. Indeed, the one she had seen coming from afar she suddenly found was beside her, and so she says: “Behold, he is behind our wall, looking out through the windows, rising above the nets. My kinsman answered and said to me: Arise, come, my near one, my beautiful one, my dove, for behold, the winter is past, the rain is gone; it has departed; flowers have appeared in the land.” The winter is the synagogue, the rain is the Jewish people, who could not see the sun, and the flowers are the apostles. And he added: “The harvest of pruning has come; the voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land.” That harvest is the faith of the Church; the voice of the turtledove is chastity.

Not only for these reasons [?], but Christ also took on the likeness of a deer because, coming to earth, he crushed that serpent the devil without any harm to himself; he offered it his heel, but did not feel its poison. Hence it was said to him: “You will walk upon the asp and the basilisk.” Let us also, then, be deer, so that we can walk upon serpents. We will be deer if we follow the voice of Christ, which prepares deer and makes them unafraid of the bites of serpents; and if any happen to be wounded, it takes away their pain by loosing their sin. Of these deer the Lord says to Job: “Have you watched over the births of the deer? Have you numbered the full months of their bearing, and eased their labor, or reared their young so that they do not fear?” Hear how the young of such deer do not fear. Let Isaiah teach you, saying: “And a little child will put his hand into the den of asps, and they will not harm him.” And so that you may recognize that he seems to mean the children of the Church, he added: “Will you send forth their offspring? Their young will break forth and multiply in their generation. They will go out and not turn back.” For no one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.

Rightly, then, the Lord became a deer, so that the voice of the Lord might prepare for himself such deer as those of whom he says: “In my name they will cast out demons, they will speak in new tongues, they will take up serpents, and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them.” For the holy apostles took up serpents when by the breath of their mouth they drove the spiritual forces of wickedness out of their hiding places in people’s bodies, and they did not feel the deadly poisons. Indeed, when a viper sprang out of the brushwood and bit Paul, the barbarians, seeing the viper hanging from his hand, thought he would suddenly die. But he stood unafraid; he was neither troubled by the wound nor filled with the poison. So, seeing him, they judged that he was above human beings, not as one born under the human condition but as one brought forth by the grace of God. See the deer drawing vipers out of their hiding places by the divine breath that was in his nostrils, as Job said.

“Paul,” it says, “turning in the spirit and looking back with grief at the spirit of divination, said: I command you in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ to come out of her at once. And it came out that very hour.” See the deer when he comes to baptism and, washed in the stream of the sacred font, casts off all the poisons of persecution. See the Lord Jesus as a deer when he came to John the Baptist; and when John said to him, “I ought to be baptized by you, and do you come to me?” he answered, “Let it be so now.” And having said this, thirsting for the salvation of all, he went down into the waters with complete eagerness. But the deer has played among us long enough at the opening of this treatise, as it does at the beginning of the year in the popular custom. Let us go on to the rest.

As I said, David appeals to the Lord, saying: "As the hart longs for the springs of water, so my soul longs for you, O God. My soul has thirsted for the living God. When shall I come and appear before the face of God?" The holy man burns with longing and cannot contain himself, for the greatness of the soul exceeds the size of any body. Untroubled in mind, he longs to fly away from earth to heaven, as he says elsewhere himself: "Who will give me wings like a dove? Then I will fly away and be at rest." For here are snares, which may not entangle the righteous man but still hinder him. Here are griefs and anxieties; there is joy, where grace is. Here, finally, are the chains of the body, which Paul was eager to loose, so that, stripped of every hindrance, he might stand free before the Lord. This, then, is what David's soul thirsted for: to see God no longer by faith but face to face, and not merely to be away from the body but to be released from it. For "to depart and be with Christ is far better," since for the righteous man "to die is gain." And it is indeed great gain to be without sin and no longer stirred by the enticements of wrongdoing. For "who is clean from filth," when not even a single day of a man's life on earth is free from the contagion of sin? By living, then, we incur losses to our innocence; by death we reach the end of error. So gain is acquired by death, while by the use of life, as with wretched debtors on a loan at interest, the interest mounts up toward guilt. And rightly does the soul thirst that hastens to the spring, not of this water, but of eternal life, of which he said above: "For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light." Rightly, then, was David hastening to come and appear before the face of God, whose countenance is light, for the Lord enlightens all on whom he looks.

"My tears," he says, "have been my bread day and night, while they say to me every day: Where is your God?" Tears are rightly bread where there is hunger for righteousness. For "blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be filled." There are, then, tears that are bread and strengthen the heart of man. The saying of Ecclesiastes also fits this discussion: "Cast your bread upon the face of the water," for where the water of grace is, there is the heavenly bread, since those from whose belly flow rivers of living water rightly receive the substance of the Word and the nourishment of mystical meaning. So too this living bread is found where there is the water of tears and the weeping of repentance. For thus it is written: "They went out in weeping, and in consolation I will bring them back."

Blessed, then, are those whose tears are bread, who have earned the right to laugh, because [?] "Blessed are you who weep." "These things I remembered," he says, "and I poured out my soul over myself." The holy man gathers himself in from external things and pours out his soul over himself, so that the soul, poured out over the body, may hide the weakness of the flesh and cover the body's appetites, and the virtue of soul and mind may spread over everything. Hence later he also says: "I will pour out my prayer in his sight." Where prayer is poured out, there sins are covered. But what does he say he remembered? Surely the things he longed for: to come and appear in the sight of God, and to see that eternal court of his, in which he walked about in spirit, delighting in an entrance he already anticipated.

"For I shall go," he says, "into the place of the wonderful tabernacle, even to the house of God, with the voice of exultation and praise, the sound of one who feasts." Not without reason did he weep at living on earth, he to whom the heavenly tabernacles were due and for whom entrance into the court of the Mighty One was waiting. Indeed, he preferred that court alone to all the riches of his kingdom, as he testified elsewhere, saying: "One thing I have asked of the Lord, this will I seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, and that I may see the delight of the Lord." The delight of the Lord is in the Church. The Church is the image of heavenly things; for after the shadow passed away, the image followed. The synagogue is the shadow: the law is in shadow, the truth in the Gospel. That is why the image of truth shines in the light of the Gospel. The prophet wept, then, because good things full of grace and brimming with joy were being put off.

Then later he also says: "Woe is me, that my sojourning is prolonged!" He appealed to the Lord because he was hastening toward better things. Yet in the very afflictions of this world there was great consolation for present things, and hope for things to come. For who would not lift up his heart if he could hope that that blessed fellowship was being kept for him in the heavenly tabernacle? But because, to our weak condition, things to come are often a weariness and things present a torment, even the soul of the holy prophet was troubled when the waves of the body rose up.

Do not be surprised that the prophet says his soul was shaken, since the Lord Jesus himself said: "Now my soul is troubled." For he who took on our weaknesses took on our feelings as well, and in them he was sorrowful even unto death, though not because of death; for a death freely chosen could not bring sorrow, a death in which the joy of all and the refreshment of all were to come. Of this he also said elsewhere: "I arose and looked, and my sleep was sweet to me." Good is the sleep that made the hungry no longer hunger and the thirsty no longer thirst, for whom he prepared the sweetness of the sacraments. How, then, was his soul troubled with fear, who made the souls of others free from fear? He was sorrowful even unto death, then, until grace should be accomplished. This is proved by his own testimony, when he says of his death: "I have a baptism to be baptized with, and how distressed I am until it is accomplished!"

Troubled, then, by the slippery windings of this world, David says: "Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me? Hope in God, for I will give him praise, the salvation of my countenance and my God." So when we are anxious and troubled, let hope strengthen us by the expectation of things to come. Look at each word. "Hope," he says, "for I will give praise": not "I give praise," but "I will give praise." That is: I shall praise him better then, when with unveiled face I behold the glory of God and am transformed into that same image.

Suddenly, while he was comforting himself, he turned back upon himself and said: "My soul is troubled within me." That is: I who ought to strengthen others am troubled myself, and since I have no firm support of my own, let us take it from the Author.

"Therefore," he says, "I will remember you, Lord, from the land of the Jordan and of Hermon." He remembers from the land of the Jordan, where grace heaps up the memory of devotion. Into the Jordan went Naaman the Syrian, and he was cleansed of leprosy. In the Jordan Christ was baptized, when he established the pattern of the saving washing. The name Jordan means "descent": the descent that the Lord Jesus made, who cleansed those living near the river Jordan from the contagion of sins. This river comes out of Egypt and divides the land of promise. So whoever is troubled, if he takes it in good part, comes out of Egypt and follows the way of light; for Hermon has been interpreted as "the way of the lamp." Come out of Egypt first, then, if you wish to see the light of Christ. The Canaanite woman came out from the borders of the Gentiles and found Christ, to whom she said: "Have mercy on me, Son of David!" Moses came out of Egypt and became a prophet, and was sent back to the people to free their souls from the land of affliction. Now the lamp of Christ is in the body. This lamp shows you the way. Hence the holy man says: "Your word is a lamp to my feet"—a lamp because it has enlightened the souls of all and shown the way in the darkness. The Gospel is the way of the lamp; it shines in the shadow, that is, in this world. Hence you also find elsewhere: "They will be made white as snow in Zalmon," that is, in the overshadowing.

Christ is also the Jordan, who divides the land. Hear how he divides: "And a sword will pierce your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed"—because he is the divider of our souls, who goes down into the inmost secrets of the heart and lays bare the thoughts of the mind. This sword is the living Word of God. Thus you read in Hebrews: "For the Word of God is living and powerful and sharper than the sharpest sword, piercing even to the dividing of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow." This is the pool of Siloam, which means "Sent," since Christ said that he was sent by the Father. There is also the division that may be gathered from the fact that tribes of the Jews lived on both banks of the Jordan. For the Son of Man, who came down from heaven in the last times, the true Jordan, the true divider of earthly and heavenly things, gave the fathers a [?] possession: one to be held on earth, the other to be kept for the merits of the life to come. Both of these befit Christ alone: to divide heavenly things and to lay bare hidden things. For he who lays bare hidden things divides what is within, and this is surely the mark of divinity. So you find it written that God said: "I will rejoice and divide Shechem." This is that splendid portion which Jacob assigned to his son Joseph as more excellent than all the rest. Hence he says: "But I give you Shechem, a splendid portion above your brothers, which I took from the hands of the Amorites with my sword and bow." This shows that the division belongs to the Lord alone, and it is grasped by the Word, that is, by that spiritual sword of the true Solomon. What does "alone" mean? The Father without Christ, or Christ without the Father? Not at all. When I say the Father alone, I do not separate the Son, because the Son is in the bosom and the secret place of the Father. When I say the Son alone, I join the Father to him as well, just as the Son joined him, saying: "Behold, the hour is coming when you will leave me alone; yet I am not alone, for the Father is with me." In the same way the Father is called "blessed and only Sovereign" without the Son being separated from him, since the Son is always in the Father. So John puts it splendidly: "In the beginning was the Word"—but he was not without the Father. And God the Father was, but he was not without the Word, because "the Word was with God."

This Shechem is the Church; for Solomon chose her, and discerned her hidden love. This Shechem is Mary, whose soul the sword of God pierces and divides. This Shechem means "ascending," as the interpretation of the name has it. Hear what it is that ascends, from what is said of the Church: "Who is she that ascends, made white, leaning on her brother?" She is active, which in Greek is called enargēs, because she shines with faith and works. To her children it is said: "Let your works shine before my Father who is in heaven."

David, then, remembers God from the land of the Jordan and of Hermon, "from the little mountain." What is this little mountain? Let us consider whether perhaps the divinity of Christ is the great mountain. Indeed, "I fill heaven and earth," says the Lord. If, then, the divinity of Christ is a great mountain, surely his incarnation is a small mountain. Christ is therefore both, the great mountain and the lesser: truly great, because "great is the Lord and great is his power"; lesser, because it is written: "You made him a little lower than the angels." Hence Isaiah says: "We saw him, and he had no form or comeliness." Yet the same one became lesser from great and great from lesser: lesser from great, because "though he was in the form of God, he emptied himself and took the form of a servant"; and great from lesser, because Daniel says: "And the stone that struck the image became a great mountain and filled the whole earth." If you ask who this stone is, recognize him: "The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner." Yet even when he seemed small, he was great. Isaiah bears witness to this, saying: "A child is born to us, a son is given to us, whose sovereignty is upon his shoulders, and he is called the Angel of Great Counsel." Christ is all things for your sake: a stone for your sake, so that you may be built up; a mountain for your sake, so that you may climb. Climb the mountain, then, you who seek heavenly things. He bowed the heavens so that you might be nearer; he rose to the summit of the mountain so that he might lift you up.

Not without reason, then, did deep call upon deep, that this mountain might become small. Of this the prophet says: "Deep calls upon deep at the voice of your cataracts." The Old Testament was not strong enough to redeem this world; it called upon the New Testament and, as it were, summoned it to its aid. The law cried out, announcing the Gospel. For it was only half complete, and so it was necessary that one should come to fulfill the law. For "Christ is the end of the law, for righteousness to everyone who believes," he who came to fulfill the law, not to abolish it. Hear how the law is a deep, from the one who says: "Your judgments are like a great deep." From this understand at the same time that both testaments belong to the one Wisdom, which he came to fulfill as his own. By the cataracts we understand the depths of the words and the force of the heavenly oracles, which have poured down on us like rain from heaven. So Christ and the divine Scripture are the remedy for every weariness and the one refuge in temptations.

Then, when David saw the swelling waves of the world coming over him—and we must pass through very many of them on the open sea of this life—he remembered the mercies of the Lord, which the Lord promised in countless oracles. Turning to prayer, he appeals to God, knowing that his mercy is commanded in the light, that is, in the law, since "your commandments are light," but that in temptations, as in the darkness of night, it is made manifest. So, like a traveler who longs to return home and reach his destination, but is worn out by the rugged road of this life, he summons a guide and begs for relief.

"With me," he says, "is prayer to the God of my life; I will say to God: You are my upholder." He rightly seeks help already familiar to him, and appeals to the author of the promise and the giver of an accustomed gift, so that in coming to his aid God, even if he finds the man's merit wanting, may not go against his own divine precedent. Someone says: "When did God take him up?" To establish this, come with me to the beginning of sacred Scripture, and see how the Lord shaped man from clay with his own hands. Hence David himself says later: "Your hands made me and fashioned me." Like a potter, God wrought the structure of human flesh. And to Jeremiah it is said: "Go down to the potter's house, and there you will hear my words." It often happens to a potter that, while a vessel is being shaped, it falls from his hands, and he gathers up the clay again to remake the vessel. So Jeremiah says: "I went down and saw how the vessel he was making fell in his hands." And again he says: "He made another vessel as it pleased him." Rightly, then, is he called upholder, because he himself took us up in his hands and himself formed us. Those are the vessels of the human potter, some for honor, some for dishonor. We are all earthen vessels: even if someone is a king, he is an earthen vessel; even if an apostle, he is a vessel. Hence Paul too says: "We have this treasure in earthen vessels." And the prophet says of a king: "Jeconiah is despised like a vessel for which there is no use." And he added: "Earth, hear the word of the Lord: write this man down as disowned." As if by a father's right, our God is accustomed to disown degenerate sons; and so the earth writes down those who are sons of the earth. That is why, when the Jews accused the adulteress, the Lord Jesus wrote with his finger on the ground. But the righteous are not written on earth, as we read. To them it is said: "Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven."

The Lord, then, took us up when he fashioned us; he takes us up also when he commands us to be born. Hence the righteous man says: "You took me up from my mother's womb." From what mother? "Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you." Those whom he forms, he also takes up; he takes them up as they come forth, too: "And before you came out of your mother's womb, I sanctified you." He is an upholder who has taken up with his hands—in this sense the maker of the human race is called upholder—and also one who has taken up by visiting, in order to protect. Hence the prophet himself says elsewhere: "He who dwells in the help of the Most High will say to the Lord: You are my upholder and my refuge." The first taking up is that of making, the second that of defending. Hear Moses, then, saying: "Spreading out his wings, he took them and bore them up on his shoulders." He took them up as the eagle does, which is accustomed to test its young, so that it may keep and rear those in whom it sees the true character of its offspring and the grace of an uncorrupted nature confirmed, or reject those in whom, at a still tender age, it detects the weakness of a degenerate origin.

"Why have you forgotten me, and why have you cast me off?" God does not forget—for it is impossible that he should forget, to whom all things, both what has been done and what is to come, are present—but our sins give him grounds for forgetting, so that he blots out those whom he has found unworthy of his visitation. For "the Lord knows those who are his." Yet to some who work iniquity he says: "I do not know you." Who, then, can say to God: "Why have you forgotten me?" And yet this is shared by the saints and by us who are weak. The holy man says it as one conscious of his merit, and yet the holier he is, the humbler he is. If even the holy man scarcely dares say it, what am I, a sinner, to say, unless I take it in this sense: Why have you forgotten your work, why have you forgotten your visitation, and finally, why have you forgotten my weakness? "For what is man, unless you visit him?" Do not, then, forget the weak. Remember, Lord, that you made me weak; remember that you fashioned me from dust. How shall I be able to stand, unless you always fix your gaze on me to make this clay firm, so that my firmness may come from your face? "When you turn away your face, all things will be troubled"; if you fix your gaze on me, woe is me. You have nothing to look at in me but the stains of sin. It does us no good to be abandoned, nor to be seen, since when we are seen we give offense. Yet we can reckon that he does not cast off those he sees, because he cleanses those he looks upon. "A fire burns before him" to burn away sin.

It is good for us, then, not to be cast off. That is why David complains: he believed that he had been cast off, though he had been taken up before. Indeed, later he said: "In you I have been strengthened from the womb." But above too we have it written: "Upon you I was cast from the womb; from my mother's belly you are my God." It is good even to be cast, but upon God. This is said in Psalm 21 in the person of Christ, who was truly cast from the Virgin's womb upon the Father; for no earthly things received him as he died. Hence, hanging on the cross, as he gave up his spirit, he said to the Father: "Into your hands I commend my spirit."

Let no one, then, add "Lord," as the psalm-singers do; I have found it neither in my Latin manuscript nor in the Greek, nor in the Gospel, which is clearer still. For earlier he had said: "Father, forgive them this sin," and so it is as to his Father that he commends his spirit into the hands of him in whose bosom the Son always is. Yet even if they add that he said "Lord," let them consider that he says this as a man facing death.

So he was cast from the womb upon the Father, "from my mother's belly"; that is, he made clear that the womb which cast him forth was his mother's belly. But the Father says: "From the womb, before the daystar, I begot you." The Father certainly did not cast off the Son, from whom the Son never went out, as he himself says: "I was handed over and did not go out." He did not cast off him to whom he is joined in the unity of the same substance. It can therefore also be read this way: "Upon you I was cast from the womb, from my mother's belly," so that what follows is: "You are my God; do not depart from me." It can also be read this way: "From my mother's belly you are my God," since even when placed in the womb I never withdrew from you; I was with you, I who, like Jonah placed in the belly of the whale, was praying to you for the people. And truly he was with God from his mother's belly, according to what is written: "For before the child knew good or evil, he chose what is good," and: "Before he could call father or mother, he plundered the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria," so that, by calling the Gentiles, he might win a kingdom for the Father through the worship of pious devotion.

Let us look at the rest. "Why," he says, "have you rejected me, and why do I go about in sorrow while the enemy afflicts me and breaks my bones? Those who trouble me have taunted me, while every day it is said to me: Where is your God? Why are you sad, my soul?" and the rest. The first plea contained a complaint that good things were being put off, things whose fruit was already longed for. The second plea was that the coming of Christ, awaited by the wise, was being delayed: the coming which the law had announced and the prophets had promised. The hearts of the righteous burned all the more impatiently because they knew that he would come for the redemption of all ...... [?] also of all, to whom by the path of the gospel he would open the way of virtue and show the paths of good works, as he himself said in Proverbs: "The Lord created me as the beginning of his ways." That is why it was said to him: "Where is your God?" For Christ had not yet come but was still hoped for. So the devil raged to crush those whom he knew would believe at the Lord's coming, and he afflicted them with various kinds of death. David therefore makes his plea, to rouse the one who delays with a prophet's lament, to urge him to hasten, and to remind him to come to our help. We have a similar plea in a later psalm as well, where the same prophet says: "O God, why have you rejected us to the end?" There he openly and tearfully laments that God has forgotten his congregation and cast away the rod of his inheritance, and that his enemies have risen up against the people of God. Of them he says: "And those who hate you have boasted in the midst of your feast." Perhaps this verse might seem to point to the Assyrians, who triumphed over the Jewish people, were it not followed by: "They set up their signs as signs, and I did not know them." Signs are always present in war: these are the standards that usually go before those about to fight and lead the army's column. Each unit or legion follows its own standards. If the soldiers are scattered in the confusion of battle, they return to wherever they see their standards, even if they are stationed far away. Each commander sets up these standards and orders that they be followed. But there are also other standards, which a victorious enemy imposes and orders to be observed, as by captives. The faithful soldier, however, follows his own standards and does not know those of others.

Let us consider more closely and carefully what these foreign signs are. Christ has placed his sign on the forehead of each person; there the Antichrist also places his signs, so that he may recognize his own. But one who is a Jew inwardly, a true confessor, says to him: "They set up their signs as signs, and I did not know them." The devil and his ministers set them up, but I did not know them, because I did not consent to his arts or give in to his commands. The Assyrian Nebuchadnezzar placed signs on the Hebrew youths. He changed their names and ordered them to worship his image, to abandon the solemn rites of their fathers, and to set aside the law of God and follow the rites of the Chaldeans. The king decreed this, but Daniel resolved in his heart to avoid the defilement of the royal table. Rightly then it suits him to say that he did not know foreign signs. The Hebrew youths had been ordered to worship the king's image, and they answered him: "We do not worship your image." Fittingly then each of them said: "They set up their signs as signs, and I did not know them": that is, I did not experience them, I did not accept them by any consent, I did not take them into myself by any fellowship. This is why we also read of the Son of God that he knew no sin. And elsewhere you have: "For whoever keeps the commandment will not know an evil word." Here it is quite clear that what is meant is not knowledge of wickedness but a share in crime. David himself also says in a later psalm: "The wicked who turned away from me I did not know." He also declares where the adversaries wished to place these signs: "As on the road," he says, "above the summit. As in a forest of trees they hacked down its doors with axes all together; with double axe and hatchet they threw it down." What does this mean, if not that our faith ought not to be as if on the road, so that the birds of the air do not come and carry it off, just as the word you read of in the gospel ought not to be sown along roads and paths?

So the adversaries, wishing to uproot this saint's faith, tried to place their signs as on the road, that is, in an open thoroughfare, because they did not see their signs in his heart. But the heart is at the summit, because "the eyes of the wise man are in his head." And they set up their signs as in a forest of trees, which are quickly burned up by fire or cut down by axes, for fire goes out from the forest and burns even the cedars of Lebanon. They thought they should do this in order to defile the tabernacle of the divine name, which is in us. For just as we are the temple of God, so we are also the tabernacle of God, in which the feasts of the Lord are celebrated. So you, O man, guard your summit, so that you may shatter the heads of the enemies, the hairy crown of those who walk about. For they walk about in superfluous things, not in holy ones: on the crown of the hair, not on the crown of devotion and faith. And "if the spirit of one who has power rises up against you," as you have it in Ecclesiastes, "do not leave your place." For Christ, who made you in the image of God, has set you on high. Hold fast, then, to the higher place of faith and piety that you received from Christ, so that, having been set above, you may easily drive back the wicked spirit as it climbs up from below, that is, from earthly and worldly things, and may not receive his signs in your breast. Do not let him occupy the forecourts of your soul or the entrances of your mind, or lay waste with his fires, as in a forest of trees, whatever is fragile and perishable, or hack down the doors of your heart with his axes. Let there be in us not a forest but a vineyard. Let the gate of our mouth and of our heart be shut with great care, so that the enemy may not enter. He quickly splits a door if he finds it open. Christ, however, knocks; he does not break it down, he who has strengthened, O Jerusalem, the bars of your gates. Christ knocks with his hand so that you may open; the adversary hacks with axes. That is why it is written that neither axe nor hammer should enter the house of God. Pride and deceit should be outside, not within; for outside there are battles, but within there is peace, which surpasses all understanding. Do not let your soul be cut by iron. Rather, as iron passed through the soul of Joseph, let it pass through your soul too, so that your ruling part, which is a kind of tabernacle of the Word, may not be torn down at the very beginning of faith, as spiritual teaching first enters. For when it is grounded by practice and training, it remains immovable and gives no room to the one who, transforming himself as it were into an angel of light, tries to climb to the summit. If he does not see his signs in us, he can have no authority to resist. So, lest the enemy afflict us and break our bones, let us not fail to persevere in Christ, so that he may say of us: "They have now been with me three days, and I do not want to send them away hungry, lest they faint on the way." Blessed is the one to whom he himself gives a firm heart, so that he cannot faint while he travels the path of this life. The one who hopes in the Lord and confesses him with his inmost heart does not faint. Even that horseman whose horse's heel the serpent bit fell backward but was not deceived, because he awaited salvation from the Lord.

The third plea is that he wishes his cause to be separated from the contagion of wicked men, since he has been placed in their midst. Many think this should be applied to the Lord Jesus, because he alone has no need to fear judgment, since he conquers when he is judged. For he faces judgment from an unjust man, and Christ enters into it willingly, as you have it written: "My people, what have I done to you, or how have I grieved you?" But since the Father has given all judgment to him, not as to one who is weak but as to his Son, what judgment can he himself undergo? If they think that the Son must undergo the Father's judgment, the Father in fact judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father. The Father honors the Son, and do you pass judgment on him? We have set this down so that no one might think we were putting the person of the prophet in the Lord's place out of fear of the question. For holy David foresaw in the Spirit that the Jews would rise up against the Lord in his passion. He does not fear judgment on his own faith, and he asks that his cause be kept apart from the race of the persecutors, so that the lineage of the whole Jewish people would not be entangled with the wicked heirs of his own race and posterity.

It is not without reason, then, that he is troubled, for he sees that he must wrestle against flesh and blood, and that within himself there is a grievous shipwreck, a storm in his own body, which he cannot withstand unless heavenly help comes to his aid. For no one is a more grievous enemy to a man than the members of his own household. And what belongs so much to a man's household as he himself and the weakness of his own flesh? That is why the prophet hurries and prays with all his heart that Christ may come. Christ is the strength of all; he would take on all our weaknesses and make the two one. By removing the dividing wall, he would end the hostility between mind and flesh as they fight against each other, for that wall divided the inner self and kept it from coming into harmony. So he had a battle within himself and another from his neighbors, who had forgotten law and justice and were preparing snares of fraud and ambushes. And the remedy he hoped for was being delayed. So he thought himself rejected, as if the one who had promised to be his remedy were refusing to come. As though called back from the hope of the dawning day into the depths of darkness, he prayed that the light would shine forth to drive away the squalor of this world, and that the eternal truth would come to abolish the deceptive image of this world.

God answered his prayers. He often comes to help when least expected and reveals himself to those who do not ask him, as he himself says: "I was revealed to those who did not seek me." Agreeing to the devout prayers, he fulfilled the whole series of requests swiftly, before they were finished. Suddenly he led the holy prophet in the spirit into the church and into his tabernacles, and set before his eyes the sacred altar on which the redemption of the whole world was to take place, along with the forgiveness of sins for all people throughout the world.

So, seeing in the spirit that sweetness of the heavenly sacraments, that table which drives back the snares of the oppressors, as he himself said earlier: "You have prepared a table before me against those who trouble me," he says: "And I will go in to the altar of my God, to God who gives joy to my youth." He spoke beautifully, as if he were Adam, when he said: "And I will go in." For we had been cast out of the Lord's paradise ever since Adam, conscious of his sin, turned away from the Lord's face. Fittingly too he added: "And I will go in to the altar of God," as though he were returning into God's sight. For God had turned away from our offerings when he did not accept the offerings of Cain, that murderer of his brother. Cain lay hidden, estranged from the Lord's sight. He was a raging, savage force of spirit, because the Lord had looked with favor on his brother's offerings, and he left his own heirs under God's displeasure. He had killed Abel, whose blood cried out to the Lord, not to his own harm alone but to the harm of us all. Hardly anyone's sacrifice was accepted any longer, because there was no one who did good, not even one, since neither faith toward God nor loving duty toward a brother was kept. The Lord Jesus came to raise up Adam, and Abel too was raised up, whose offerings pleased God. The Lord Jesus offered himself, that is, the firstfruits of his body, in the sprinkling of blood that speaks better than the blood of Abel spoke on the earth. God looked with favor on his offerings, and from this he himself left the grace of divine reconciliation to good heirs. Rightly then holy David says, as if speaking for reconciled humanity: "And I will go in to the altar of my God, to God who gives joy to my youth."

Let us support this passage, if we can, with the example of another prophet as well, to show how the Lord first turned away from man's sacrifices and was afterward reconciled to him. We have it written in the book of Isaiah, where God says: "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices? says the Lord. I am full." That is: I have plenty of my own; I do not seek yours. "Burnt offerings of rams, the fat of lambs, the blood of bulls and goats I do not want; do not come into my sight like this." And yet Abel had offered a sacrifice from the young of his flock, and with it he had pleased God. But the one who was waiting for the true sacrifice did not require the type, for the saving passion of the Lord was awaited. "For who," he says, "required these things from your hands? You shall no longer trample my courts." And further on: "When you stretch out your hands to me, I will turn my face away from you. But wash yourselves, be clean, remove the wickedness from your souls. Give judgment for the orphan and justice to the widow, and come, let us reason together, says the Lord." It is clear, then, that the Lord first turned away from man's sacrifices and was afterward reconciled, so that he deigned to look with favor on our sacrifices.

Therefore whoever goes in to the Lord's mercy enters without fear. Thus it is said to the good servant: "Enter into the joy of your master," but of the wicked servant it is said: "Take him away into the outer darkness." That is why Adam too, cast out of the heavenly homeland and the dwelling of paradise, was banished to the island of sin. Rightly then Scripture says: "Be renewed, O islands," because we are surrounded by the waves of sin like islands in the strait of this world. These islands were renewed by the forgiveness of sins through the Lord's coming. That is, people placed [?] in the washing, in the midst of the waters, like islands, were pounded by masses of waves, as islands are by the roaring breakers of sin dashing against them. They were like islands where formerly the simple suffered frequent shipwreck, as on reefs of deceit, because there was guile in the heart and flattery on the lips. But then the Lord Jesus, in whom there is no guile, came into this world. By setting out heavenly teaching he calmed the depths of human minds, poured tranquility back into each person's heart, and removed the hedge of discord. After that, havens, as it were, began to offer refuge to those who approached, so that each might moor the vessel of his rest in the love of his neighbor or brother, and hold fast to the shore in the sheltered retreat of a devout mind.

It is not without reason, then, that David cries out like one renewed: "And I will go in to the altar of my God, to God who gives joy to my youth." Earlier, as we read in the sixth psalm, he had said that he had grown old among his enemies; here he says that his youth has been renewed, after the worn-out old age brought on by man's fall. For we are renewed through the washing of regeneration, we are renewed through the outpouring of the Holy Spirit, and we shall also be renewed through the resurrection, as he says in a later psalm: "Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle's." Hear how we are renewed: "You will sprinkle me with hyssop and I shall be clean; you will wash me and I shall be whiter than snow." And in Isaiah he says: "Though your sins are like scarlet, I will make them white as snow." Rightly is he renewed who is changed from the darkness of sins into the light of virtue and grace, so that he who was once filthy with foul defilement may shine with a radiance whiter than snow.

"I will praise you on the lyre, my God." Our soul has its own lyre. Paul would not say: "I will pray with the spirit, I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, I will sing with the mind also," unless he had a lyre that resounded under the plectrum of the Holy Spirit. Our flesh is a lyre when it dies to sin so that it may live to God; it is a lyre when it receives the sevenfold Spirit in the sacrament of baptism. While the tortoise is alive, it is sunk in mud; once it has died, its shell is fitted for making music and for the grace of devout discipline, so that it may sound out the seven distinct tones in measured rhythms. In the same way our flesh, if it lives amid bodily enticements, lives in a kind of mire and whirlpool of pleasures. But if it dies to luxury and lack of self-control, then it takes up true life, then it begins to give forth the sweet melody of good works. Sweet is the sound of chastity, sweet the sound of those who fear God. Indeed, "their sound has gone out into all the earth." Sweet is the sound of faith, which is proclaimed, as it is written, in the whole world. Let this sound go out from us to God, as it also went out from the Thessalonians, so that even when we are not singing we may sing, and proclaim the Lord through the harmony of good works. To him be honor, glory and eternity from before the ages, now and always and for all ages of ages. Amen.
